Hi, my name is Scott Garrison and I am fundraising for my puppy Atlas. Atlas is a four month old black Labrador mix and was diagnosed with parvovirus on Thursday. Parvovirus is a disease that rapidly attacks the gastrointestinal track of a dog and is very fatal in puppies. Most puppies die within the first 24-72 hours of the disease and without treatment, the fatality rate exceeds 90 percent. With hospital treatment, however, the survival rate is around 90 percent.
The first day he was diagnosed, I decided to do outpatient care as his case wasn’t terrible and I was advised it was a valid option for him. He had only been showing symptoms for about a day so we had caught it early on. I took a few days off from work as I was told his case was going to get worse over the next couple days as the disease progressed and he needed to be monitored and cared for. Atlas was very stubborn when it came to taking his medicine and would hold it or gag till he almost vomited so I was only able to successfully get him to take a couple of his medications. I was also told to entice him to eat in any way possible but he just refused anything I tried to give him, treats included.
The next morning he was starting to show that he was doing worse and so I decided I was going to bring him back and admit him to the hospital for inpatient care since I couldn’t get him to eat or take medicine. I was called later that night and informed that he wasn’t doing well and would most likely pass before I could make it to the hospital. His blood glucose levels had dropped to an unreadable level and he had become unresponsive. As a result, I rushed there and sat with him and was preparing for the worst. He did, however, try moving around and lifted his head upon seeing me. I was advised that euthanizing him wouldn’t be the wrong choice but neither would holding out till the morning. I decided to wait till the morning to say I at least gave it everything I could and they started putting him on an almost purely sugar solution in hopes of raising his sugar levels.
Atlas did stabilize and his sugar levels reached a normal level yesterday. They started weening him off of the sugar solution and his levels stayed up. He even got up and moved around a few times throughout the day, wagging his tail and being a bit more active. With the highs also came some lows and so it’s been an up and down but he is fighting very hard for his life.
Today the initial deposit ran out and so he was stopped his treatment. I was told that because of all the help he was being given currently, he wouldn’t be able to survive at home most likely and so I was again faced with the decision of euthanizing or putting another deposit down for 48 more hours. The bills have been piling up because it is such intensive care. I have exhausted my personal funds, opened up new lines of credit such as a CareCredit card, and borrowed money from family to pay for this. I don’t like asking for money, but in this case I don’t have much of a choice. Any donations are greatly appreciated or even just sharing would help immensely.
Thank you all very much. Atlas is one of the best dogs I have ever met. He is so loving and playful and has such an amazing temperament that he deserves to have a chance at life. He has become my best friend so quickly and I can’t imagine not having him with me. Even these past couple days have been such an adjustment and I find myself just calling to him or doing things out of habit. As long as Atlas isn’t giving up, neither am I.

Thank you for caring enough to be here reading this right now. I’d like to kindly ask for a few more minutes of your time so I can share a little bit more about Daisey Mae, our 11 year journey, and the current situation we have landed as we hope for a fighting chance- together.  
On December 9th, 2011 my Dad was killed in front of me after being struck by a car while crossing the street. The weeks that followed were a blur of shock, denial, despair, complete heartbreak and emptiness - until one day I found a tiny glimmer of hope.  I stumbled on a Facebook post of golden retriever puppies needing homes by Christmas. I already had one furchild, Koby, but after seeing those faces I couldn’t stop thinking about them. I decided I would just go look (famous last words), despite everyone telling me I ‘didn’t need another dog’. 
I picked one up, then another, then another. Sure they were adorable, but they weren’t …mine. I thought- maybe it wasn’t meant to be after all. Until right at that moment….I noticed a tiny sleepy one. Her chubby belly up pointed to the sky, paws going all directions, all tucked away in a corner. 
As soon as I picked her up she opened her tired eyes and looked at me with complete and utter disbelief, like she couldn’t believe I had inconvenienced her like this. She quickly crossed her tiny puppy paws, one on top of another, and stared off into the distance. The. SASS. I immediately burst into laughter. The first time since December 9th that I felt anything other than broken, empty pain. I knew immediately, ‘This is her.’ 
Since then, Daisey Mae became my ray of sunshine in what felt most days like suffocating darkness. The comedic relief and gentle spirit I so desperately needed to survive my 20’s as I moved to a brand new city alone. She became Koby’s best friend and we became an inseparable unit of 3. She was by my side while I navigated the heaviness of grief, PTSD, severe depression and crippling anxiety. She constantly distracted me with her ability to literally give no shits about anything, ever, in the most pure and mindlessly magical way. Never phased by the years of small apartments, or the countless moves we made around Nashville until I could give them what they always deserved: Their very own yard.  Freedom to run. And finally-home that was ours. 
A lot of people consider their dogs to be family, but for me, they are quite literally all I have. It’s been them and I against the world, in our own little corner of the world, every single day, night, weekend, and holiday for over a decade. It’s always been us, and only us. 
My dogs have single-handily saved me in every sense of the word. And now it’s time for me to save her.
I want to give Daisey Mae the best possible chance I can. While making the least selfish decisions - because I know that no time will ever be enough. But she deserves as much time as I can fight for her to have. As much time as I can give her to still be the giant happy goof ball that she is. 
So now, as we navigate Daisey’s newly diagnosed Thyroid Carcinoma and begin to learn her prognosis, options and treatments: This fund is for her. 
We thank you from the bottom of our hearts for any support you can give. Even the tiniest bit can and will help. I hope to have positive updates sooner than later.

Betzy is a very special pup. She sparks joy wherever she wiggles with her gremlin crawl. Betzy has become somewhat of a local celebrity on the Upper West Side. She has a little fan club. Wherever her Mommy, Robyn (also an UWS staple), takes Betzy, New Yorkers gush over her. Kids are especially drawn to Betzy’s sweet nature. She’s impossible to resist. There is something warm and joyful about Betzy- maybe she knows she was given a second chance. 
Betzy was found on the side of the road in Hartwell, GA on May 27th this year.  The vet believes she was hit <very badly> by a car and left. Her left leg was amputated  as well as her tail because she had bone exposed, which causes her a lot of pain. Sadly Betzy’s other hind leg was also impacted by the hit and run. They wanted to give her a chance and “only” amputated one leg with the hopes that she would go to physical therapy to rehabilitate what was left by her rear limbs. 
On August 7th, Betzy met her Mommy, Robyn, thanks to Second Chance Rescue NYC. Robyn was no match for Betzy's charm. Having weathered the storm of a heavy and trying few years, Robyn was moved by Betzy's strength and resiliency. They were instantly connected and ready to take on the world.
On their very first morning walk, a good samaritan named, Avi, witnessed Robyn and Betzy's interactions, their good hearts, and how they treated others. Avi said there’s a word in Hebrew called “Bashert” which means “Destiny” and said he felt Robyn and Betzy were each others Bashert. He then gifted Betzy $1,000 for her first water therapy sessions, which is the ideal therapy for “tripod” pups to heal and thrive.  After only four sessions Betzy started to improve and can now stand on her back leg and even run for short periods of time.
While the water therapy has helped immensely, Betzy's recovery process now needs additional care because she is resilient AF and so playful. Betzy now needs to get wheels and a hind leg prosthetic which is very rare.  As a New Yorker pupper, this will provide a greater quality of life for Betzy to explore the rest of the city, without the constant "commute" stress.
Betzy is a regular at Riverside Park and loves to watch the squirrels, but her favorite is the dog park. Robyn typically brings her for 1-2 hours before she starts work for the day and again after work.  The Dogpark goers have fallen in love with Betzy and always look out for her. Betzy’s favorite game is tugowar and she usually finds a stick or rope toy in the park to bombard her dog friends until they play with her. Some of the dog parents said their dogs never played tugowar until Betzy “taught” them. 
Betzy also likes to people watch. She often will sit down and just watch everyone pass by, say hi to the kids with a nose kiss or 5,  and sidewalk play wrestle with other pups. The local businesses now know her by name - especially her “bodega cat” which she visits about 4x daily. 
Robyn met another “Tri-pawd” fur mama at the dog park and she introduced them to the founders of 3D Pets, Alex and Adam. Betzy met with them in early October and they are going to make her a custom state of the art prosthetic leg on her left side and also attach a wheel (think training wheel) to her right side to support her leg while she is working to strengthen it in PT. 
Understandably, this process has been very costly. PT sessions run up to $200 a session (with insurance) and the prosthetic will cost over $2,000.  
If you are receiving this note, it's likely that Robyn and Betzy have either warmed your heart or are very special to you. Please consider contributing to Betzy’s recovery, in the name of second chances and nurturing a spirit that sparks joy for so many.

I'm Ido, and I have an 18.5-year-old cat named Haku. She has been battling chronic kidney disease and has reached the end stage (kidney failure), among other discomforts such as irregular heartbeat, arthritis, and a possible cancerous mass found in her most recent vet visit.
After consultation with the vet, it has been determined that any treatment will only buy her a few weeks to maybe a month or two at most. Therefore, I've decided to opt for euthanasia over a natural death. These donations will be going towards the cost of the procedure, cremation, and the return of her ashes.
Any extra donations will go towards the best food, treats, and pampering I can give her.
Her appointment with the local Anti-Cruelty Society for the procedure is set for Tuesday, Oct. 18.
Why euthanasia?
For some people, the thought of an aided death for a pet may seem stomach-churning. Plenty of senior cats pass on peacefully at home. Unfortunately, when it comes to cats with CKD, it is less likely to be pleasant.
With CKD comes a lot of pain and discomfort. We adopted Spirit, formerly Summer, from Berkeley County Animal Shelter in early July of 2022. She is now 7.5 months old. She started having substantial issues with pain and mobility a couple of months after we adopted her. After a visit to a family vet, she was given a preliminary diagnosis of Steroid Responsive Meningitis. This was after we had paid over $1500 on diagnostic tests to rule out other causes. This is an auto-immune disease where the body attacks its own central nervous system and almost exclusive occurs in dogs under 2 years of age. The confirmation tests for Steroid Responsive Meningitis are expensive and carry some risk, so the vet suggested the best way to find out was to see if she responded to steroids. On steroids she was improving!
The family vet still recommended she be seen by a specialty vet, so that is what we did. The specialist disagreed with the diagnosis and said we take over off steroids. It is a slow process because you gradually have to reduce the dosage. It wasn't until she was receiving a low dosage of steroids every other day that she had a major relapse in the form of a disease flare up, which landed her in the emergency hospital for 3 nights. She couldn't walk at all and was in an incredible amount of pain, so much that she had to be on a continuous pain medication drip and was close to crashing, which is why she had to stay. After more tests that did not provide additional definitive diagnoses, we had to insist that they put her back on high-dose steroids and she started improving within 24 hours. Now she is back at home and continuing to improve every day because she is back on the same treatment she was on originally.  
Her hospital stay and preliminary diagnostics have cost us over $6,000. I have included the bill from her hospital stay. We love and adore our girl and are committed to helping her fight this. She also has a big brother (Thunder) and they have already bonded (pictures included)!
The prognosis for this disease is good and the treatment (steroids) is not that expensive. We also need to find a vet that has experience treating this as we will not be going back to the "specialist". Hi everyone,For those of you who may or may not know, heartworm is a potentially fatal disease that is contracted through a mosquito bite. Worms are then spread and inhabit a dogs heart, lungs, and associated blood vessels. It is entirely preventable but when living in poor conditions and under poor care, it’s frequently caught. Dogs who are then diagnosed with heartworm disease can suffer from severe lung disease, heart failure, other organ damage, and potentially death. Detecting heartworm as early as possible and treating it promptly allows for dogs to fully recovery and still live a normal, healthy life. We currently have 6 dogs who are heartworm positive and will either require, have begun, or just completed treatment. Treatment ranges anywhere from $500 to $1,500 per dog. Each dog sat at the shelter on the euth list, and a huge part had to do with their heartworm results since funds are limited for so many rescues. To name a few:Momma Summer - she carried, birthed, and cared for 12 puppies all while being heartworm positive. She arrived in horrific condition, yet remained the most resilient momma ever. Daisy & Sadie - purebred Dobermans who were surrendered by their AKC breeder to a kill shelter. The breeder had too many females/puppies and did not want the risk of any more. Both were bred while being heartworm positive.Maia - dumped by her family of 2 years because they didn’t want to deal with the stress of moving with a dog. Hi, my name is Brittni and I am working together with a couple of my wonderful neighbors to raise money for the colony of cats in our neighborhood.
All of you that know me know the story of my sweet girl Clementine who’s mom cried out for help outside my house when she got stuck during a wind storm. You’ve followed our story as she has become the light of my life, my hiking and travel companion; But what most of you didn’t get to see is the story of her mother, Mia. A beautiful tortie girl who’s lived a very tough life in a very short period of time.
After that brutally windy night in January I tried for weeks to lure, coax and trap Mama Mia and another kitten I thought had run off with her. Back then I didn’t know much about cats and how to go about doing such things so with no luck and winter hitting I gave up, assuming they had moved on. Well, about a year ago when Clementine went missing I set up a camera and with that camera came back Mia and more! I have been feeding them ever since thinking that I was helping them and I was, but a couple months ago I learned I was there to do much more. Mia came one night, as always, but this time she was pregnant and had no tail! I was horrified. I immediately sprung into action, got myself a trap and caught her. I was able to find a great organization called operation pets to help her at a reduced rate. They were able to amputate the remaining tail, stitch her up AND determine that she was not pregnant! However, she had just given birth there was a 4-6 week old litter out there somewhere.
Again, I immediately sprung into action to find them. Upon my search I ran into a man on a neighboring street. Outside on his porch feeding and playing with about multiple kittens. We connected and he told me the story of who we now call Mia.
Mia was left behind by a neighbor 4 years ago. An unfixed cat that got out on their moving day. They had no time stay around and try and find her- nor create posts or alert other neighbors. Mia is not a feral or an outdoor cat. She is a sweet tiny tortie girl who proved that night when she called out for her kitten to be saved that she is an indoor people loving cat! In those 4 years Mia has been roaming the streets, scared, having litter after litter who then goes on to have litter after litter, and now with no tail.
Starting at 4 months of age cats can have up to 4 kittens in a litter up to 5 times a year for their entire lives! Every time you think you see 1 stray kitten their are 15-25 more in only 1 colony and a 2nd colony could be only a couple streets away.
We have watched day old litters die after being left behind, kittens get hit by cars, attacked by dogs; even raccoons and foxes that come from the cemetery and we just cannot stand by and watch anymore.
My point is, as humans, humane beings. We all need to do our part. Some can give money, so can give time, some can give love. Any little thing helps.
We have reached out to multiple organizations but unfortunately there is not enough volunteers/foster or funding to keep up with the rapid rates at which these animals are producing. So my neighbors and I our asking our friends and community for help in our efforts of fixing and rehoming the cats of OUR community. We are looking to get all kittens and cats we find fixed with shots to prevent disease spreading. All feral cats will be returned to the streets and it is the life they have chose and the one that is best for them. All friendly’s will be given a foster home until we are able to find them their forever home. (We have a couple right now if you’re looking to adopt)
Please donate and share this page in an effort to prevent these colonies and to give these adorable animals a chance at life.
Thank you so much in advance from the bottom of our hearts,
The Inwood/ Potomac/ Delaware community

On October 24, three exhausted volunteers arrived at the animal shelter at which they volunteer. They needed to do evening rounds: scooping litter boxes, giving medication to cats with colds and diarrhea, and making sure every one of the almost 30 cats at the shelter had food, water, and some face time with a person who loves them.
That same day, they had rushed a batch of kittens from their foster home to a vet, where two of them were ultimately lost.
This has been woefully common this year. Kittens are so vulnerable to illness, and when they start to turn, it can be very fast - and very hard to bring them back. Collectively, the team has lost over a dozen kittens in the past two months. Each death hits deep.
So, exhausted both physically and emotionally, one of the volunteers brought a bag of scooped litter to the trash outside - and then she heard a chorus of tiny meows.
From a closed Tupperware container on the ground. Outside. Next to the trash.
No note. No call. No food in the container. Just nine 3-4 week old kittens, left there alone on the night of the first snow of this season.
Nine currently healthy, beautiful, playful, affectionate kittens, who were rushed into a foster home with the volunteer who found them. The team rallied to get them fed, cleaned up, checked on, and through their first night. All of them are still healthy, beautiful, playful, affectionate - and now that the emergency is fading to the background of so many other days like it, we have to figure out how to care for them.
They'll need to be spayed/neutered, so $500 of this will cover that for them. We have access to a low-cost program, thankfully! The other $500 will go to vaccines and microchips. This is only the beginning, the baseline of healthcare that we need to offer them... and we need your help. Nine unexpected cats is a lot for our small, tired team, but we're here for them.
No kitten is trash. Each one is a life, and we're going to give our all to save them all. Can you help Karley, Hannah, Rachel, and me to do that?

On Monday night, October 24th, our 10-month-old puppy, Sherman, threw up his dinner. We didn't think much of it at first, but he kept throwing up, over and over, into the following morning. We tried giving him water, but that kept coming up, too. Worried, we took Sherman to the vet, who gave him some intervenous hydrating fluids and anti-nausea medication. We thought this would solve the problem. However, as the day progressed, Sherman had no appetite for food. He was still interested in drinking water but kept throwing up after every sip. He was getting increasingly sluggish and uncomfortable, and we were getting scared.
Upon returning to the vet, it was recommended that we take him to an emergency clinic so a team of doctors could triage the situation and identify the cause of these symptoms. Since the anti-nausea medication wasn't working and Sherman wasn't interested in eating, they recommended that we check him in to stay the night, where he could be monitored in case the situation worsened. We agreed. They were also concerned that there could be a blockage somewhere in his digestive tract. They attached a catheter to medicate him intravenously and took X-rays and blood samples for lab work. 
At around 4 a.m. the following morning, we received a call from the doctors, recommending we approve their request to run a NasoGastric tube through Sherman's nose to his stomach. That way, they would be able to feed and hydrate Sherman effectively (since he hadn't eaten in 3 days) and use the line to clear the fluid buildup in his stomach to reduce his nausea. We approved the request, and Sherman quickly started to improve. However, the X-rays and lab work still didn't clarify the cause of the problem. Additional X-rays and ultrasounds were given, and more tests were run.
We visited Sherman daily, bringing him food (hoping he would eat) and giving him lots of love and warm pets. On Friday morning, the doctor identified a high level of vitamin C in his blood. It was approaching toxic levels. She believed this could be the cause of Sherman's situation. Once given medicine to help reduce the Vitamin C levels, Sherman's appetite began to return. He still had to be fed most of his food through his NasoGastric tube, but he was starting to snack little by little on the food the technicians were setting out for him. I came to visit the following day, and his tail was wagging again (which it hadn't done in the past week). He ate two treats right out of my hand! We were overjoyed! 
Still, Sherman needed two more nights at the doctor's before his natural appetite was back, his nausea resolved, and everyone felt comfortable and safe enough to send him home (with medication, of course). We're still not sure what the cause of this episode was. The doctors think it could either be Addison's disease or that his own body could have caused the surplus due to the recent growth spurt he is currently having. We are awaiting test results, which we hope will provide answers and clarify how we best care for our sweet pup from now on.
In the meantime, Sherman has been recovering quickly back at home. He has forgotten some potty training rules (he'll remember them soon), but he is taking his medicine like a champ, eating his meals, drinking water, and gaining energy back. Sherman is feeling much better. And he's slowly warming up to playing fetch in the yard again. We're ecstatic to have him back home, healthy, comfortable, and cozy after such an ordeal. We can only imagine how scary and confusing it was for him. We were scared, too. In two weeks, we'll have his next doctor's appointment to review the test results and plan for the future.
We have pet insurance, which I recommend, especially after an ordeal like this. However, we're already extremely close to hitting our maximum number of claims since Sherman also needed his vaccinations, neutering, microchipping, and other routine puppy vet visits this year. This specific "adventure" has cost us close to $12,000 out-of-pocket all on its own.
This bill is hard to pay off, and while we don't expect anything, we wanted to create a GoFundMe to see what might be possible with the help and support of others. It's always awkward to do something like this. We don't expect to receive the total amount we've asked for. However, if we surpass that amount, every additional cent will go towards any future medical bills Sherman has related to this event. Suppose this turns out to be a one-off situation (which we hope) that does not require long-term care or if our Pet Insurance is able to reimburse for more than we expect. In that case, everything additional will be donated to the Wagmor Pets Dog Rescue to help other doggies in need. 
Sherman, Sarah, and I appreciate you taking the time out of your day to read this as well as anything you may be able to give.

In January 2022, we rescued a retired dairy cow named Potekoro. We support Potekoro financially via my group Vegmama (an online Japanese moms group that studies Plant Based nutrition ) with the help of a dairy farmer in Hokkaido who raised Potekoro.
At first, our goal was to transition the dairy farm to a cow sanctuary and sustainable vegetable farm in 5 to 10 years.  Unfortunately, due to the struggling Japanese dairy industry, Potekoro's caretaker must sell the farm by the end of 2022.

I am asking for donations so I can at least take Marvin to the vet for a checkup and x-rays. We do not have enough extra money to care for this neighborhood cat. We will also be putting some toward his care but not as much as he will need. 
This sweet boy means so much to me. My hope is to get him better and keep him safe so he can live much longer.

Hi there! I’m Nicole, but you might know me better as Backyard Cats of Bed-Stuy. 
Today I’d like to tell you a little bit about a handsome black panther, aptly named T’Challa. T’Challa was given his name by Hannah and Shivana, two incredibly kind and caring fellow cat-loving  Brooklynites who found a gentle boy on the street in Flatbush and knew in their hearts he didn’t belong there. A couple of degrees of separation later they found me, and we immediately set to work getting T’Challa to a vet for all the basics and finding him a more permanent foster home.
T’Challa and I were incredibly lucky that Hannah and Shivana were willing to give him a place to crash for a couple of weeks while all of that could happen. We were even luckier to meet Scott, who so graciously welcomed T’Challa as his new roommate. As it turns out, rent in Brooklyn is out of control, so Scott allows T’Challa to cover his portion with snuggles and meows. (Maybe the best deal in all of NYC!)
I’ve had the immensely rare fortune to not face many rescue bills I felt *too* daunted by, but truthfully since T’Challa is a senior guy, and undeniably an abandoned pet, it’s not too surprising that his prognosis isn’t straightforward. He will undoubtedly need a dental cleaning/extraction, but before he can even be scheduled for that, he’ll need to see a cardiologist for a low-grade heart murmur. T’Challa was also very thin upon intake, so he’s on the best-of-the-best food in order to fatten him up without causing his mouth too much pain. I normally shy away from asking for monetary donations, because there are so many rescuers out there that do so much more on far less, but T’Challa’s vet visits alone have already cost me upwards of $500. His cardiologist visit will be around $800, and his dental another $1000 or so. We may still have a long road ahead of us to get this guy in tip-top shape again, but I’m fully committed to helping this sweet old man live his best life. Anything you can spare will go straight to T’Challa’s care. 
Thank you my friends

Hi. This is for my furbaby, Yuri. In the timespan of just three weeks, Yuri has spent three nights in the hospital and seven days on IV fluids on and off. She had come home needing anywhere between six through nine different medications throughout the day, and each with their own complicated set of instructions. e.g. give with food, give with no food, give two hours before or after any other medication on an empty stomach. It is so complicated that her vet makes hospital treatment sheets to record how and when I give her medications. 
This all began about a year and a half ago when Yuri started urinating blood a few hours after being taken out for a walk. She was treated multiple times for a UTI before a doctor found out that it wasn’t blood in her urine. It was pigment. After waiting three weeks for results from a special laboratory in Pennsylvania, we found out that Yuri is probably the first German Spitz to be diagnosed with a rare, autosomal recessive genetic disorder called PhosphoFructoKinase deficiency. This disease is one where any type of activity, stress, play, and even panting can result in the destruction of her red blood cells. This in turn would cause her urine to turn red and yellow. In the middle of October, it got so bad that her urine turned black. Since then, she has been treated for hypertension, pancreatitis, cholangiohepatitis, and jaundice. She was also presumed to have immune mediated hemolytic anemia, but once she tested positive for PFK, we have slowly started taking her off steroids in hope that she only has the PFK deficiency, though there may be multiple issues going on that complicate her case. 
The doctors tell us that from now on Yuri needs to live a quiet life with minimal activity. She just turned three years old and we are told it is possible her life span may be normal. But she will have ups and downs of anemia for the rest of her life. We hope you may be able to help us support Yuri’s current crisis and start planning for her future care and comfortability. 
Thank you! 
Megan

Hello everyone. 
Anyone who knows any member of our apartment has surely been subjected to hearing all about our sweet boy, Ricky. Since March of 2021, this little dude has brought nothing but joy to our lives, and in return, we’ve spoiled him rotten, showering him with love, affection, and his favorite - Greenies cat treats. 
Unfortunately, about a month ago, we noticed Ricky seemed to be getting sick. We thought for a few weeks that he just had a cold - he was sniffly, had a hard time eating, and wasn’t doing his usual midday zoomies around the apartment. After 2 weeks of the cold not clearing up, we took him to the vet - that’s when they told us that the situation was far more dire than simply a cold - our little dude was suffering from FIP (Feline Infectious Peritonitis). In most cases, FIP is fatal, with a prognosis of only a few weeks, or a few months if we were lucky. 
Because he is so young, and was an extremely healthy little dude prior to this, he’s a great candidate for an experimental (and extremely effective) treatment. Unfortunately experimental also means expensive… so here we are. 
Between the medication itself, the supplies for his injections, and the numerous vet visits it’ll take to run blood tests, check out his vitals, etc, we are looking at a hefty bill - one that 3 baristas and a grad student can’t manage on our own. 
We know money is tight for everyone right now, especially with the holidays right around the corner, and asking for help is hard - but Ricky has brought endless joy to our lives for the last year and a half, and the thought of losing him is unimaginable. He’s the main character of our apartment, a screaming little goblin who demands the attention of everyone in the room. He’s barely 2 and a half, and we’re confident that if we can get him through treatment, we’ll get many more years with him. 
We appreciate you reading this far, and please know that whatever help you’re able to offer, whether it’s a donation or simply sharing the link, we are so, so appreciative.

Many people were left homeless and with nothing. Some losing their lives. One of those people who will soon be without a home is my sister, Vicki Schmand. While she has held out hope that her complex will be spared, that doesn’t appear to be. She lives on Daytona Beach Shores. She watched as this storm did not move for up to 8 hours, gaining momentum as it sat. She has never seen a storm this big. She had taken all precautions that were needed.
Vicki is 65 and her income is social security disability. She has lived in her apartment for 12 years. And in Florida for 17. She had established herself there. She had her two dogs, Shrek and Fiona, and her two cats, Calvin and Hobbs. She was, and has been, comfortable and had no plans to move.
When this storm hit, it tore a roof off the lower section of the complex. This, in turn, ripped the power lines from the building. She has had no power since the date of the storm. About a month now. There was a thought of connecting temporarily, but there was too much damage inside from extreme winds and rain that came in sideways and under the boards on the windows. This ruined her queen size bed (mattress and boxspring), furniture and carpeting she had, plus other items. This is where she is at. The insurance company would not go for a temporary hookup to the pole.
She has done what she could to stay. She has been in contact with FEMA repeatedly. With that said, this is where she is at. Her dogs, Shrek and Fiona, are 18 years old. They have lived a very good and long life. Shrek has congestive heart. She cannot keep him as cool as he needs and had to make the very hard decision to have a vet come in and euthanize. Fiona also has some health issues. And she cannot, in Fiona’s best interest, leave her without her brother. She knows it’s time. This has been the hardest thing she has ever done.
As far as a home is concerned…she has many people looking for a camper or trailer that she can stay in temporarily. FEMA has gathered up most of those for the many displaced people. Rents have hit the roof and they are not cheap. She needs to stay within her means. She feels this may be the best decision. There doesn’t seem to be anything else popping up and without AC or power, the heat is becoming unbearable. Recently she has looked at getting a camper and this is the most feasible decision. Where she lost all furniture, these are already set up. One has come up and she would just need the little asked for to complete a purchase. It would be hers and paid for. She also has a place to set it up more inland with a friend.
This is family, and this is also an immediate and emergent issue.
She has her two cats who are her main concern.
So we have set up this fund to help. She has been asked by multiple people where the GoFundMe is so they can help.
She told me that the waiting and not knowing what she will do is probably the worst. She sits and thinks and there are no answers. And we all know that that is one of the hardest things. Waiting to see if there is a fix or if there is another shoe dropping. She is stressed, she is tired, and she worries. And we thought this will help alleviate that in at least a small way.
We have set a goal. And it is not astronomical and she would not ask for more than she needs. This will help get a camper that is decent sized.
To cover two questions people seem to have:
1.	She had her two dogs put down. How could she afford that? My husband and I gave her that money. It’s not cheap to have a vet come and do this. We covered it as she had no other choice.
2.	How come she did not evacuate when told? Well, they were never informed. It was listed as a tropical storm, and the town has been through many with no real issues. It was not until it came across the state and too late that anyone realized that was not the case. There was no evacuation, and at that point, the bridges got shut down to the peninsula. So everyone in town hunkered down, took precautions, she had all the tenants clear anything out they had outside and boarded windows. It could not have been known that this storm would sit and spin and gain the power it did over Daytona Beach Shores. It was decided by contractors doing the work in the area that a tornado had spun off from the storm just sitting, and that is what did the damages they had.
So, please read to the bottom for the most current slap in the face. Vicki is trying to get it straightened out. But needs FEMA to see the damage. She is the only one left at the apartment complex who has not been seen. Even when they come, they can’t just take care of hers. She has to be by appointment only, so she can't do anything when they go to the other tenants. And most all now are gone.
UPDATE TO THIS POST: Vicki was contacted by FEMA. They were to come in Saturday, October 15th, and do the inspection. They did not show. She finally got through to them yesterday and they rescheduled for Tuesday ,October 18th. That was great to hear. HOWEVER: she received a text from FEMA and they said to check her account for status? Well, she has no status at the moment besides limbo land. So she did. And it stated the inspection was complete…basically found no damage and there will be no funds given!!! She is totally pissed (sorry, there is no other word at the moment). She is on hold with them and the woman on the line said “what?!” and put her through to talk with whomever. BUT…she said if they closed it then she couldn’t do anything.
She was going on 21 days of no power. She did, in fact, get in touch with a supervisor who saw all that was in the records and could not believe how basically botched up it got for no reason. There was no proof of anything they had said. So, she was put back in the system. Again, taking more time to hurry up and wait.
SECOND UPDATE: An inspector finally came on Friday, October 21st.
She stated her place was a complete loss and filed it as needing all new furniture, miscellaneous, and the funds to move that FEMA allocates. However, when she again checked the status, it stated that she refused the relocation funds, which she did not. She again calls the supervisor, who clearly saw the report that she needed it and, again, had no idea why it was not included and omitted as refused. She was told to FAX her appeal with that information on Monday morning immediately. And she did this. Now she is told it could be another month before she sees that funding. She has now been a month without electric. She would love to have her own place again and be in it for Thanksgiving. And have power once again.
Getting the camper, she would own it, and it would show something she has instead of renting for crazy money and not having anything to show. So if you can, please donate to help her out. Every little bit will help.
I will update this as she learns more of what is going on. And Please....share...share...share.

On Friday, October 28, 2022 my 70-year-old dad, Alan Ash, was a victim of a high-speed, head-on collision just outside of Deming, New Mexico. He is my hero and my rock and I am beyond grateful that he survived. Due to his injuries, he is facing an indeterminate amount of time off of work from his beloved profession as a Stonemason. 
Dad lives and works on the road, so this devastating event - which totaled both his truck and travel trailer - has also left him homeless and 1600 miles from home base in Oregon. 
As we have been navigating the challenges of this tragic situation, it has become apparent that his immediate need is financial support. 
 
The financial impacts of losing both vehicles is especially difficult. Dad had just put a brand-new, factory-remanufactured, 12-valve Cummins engine into his ‘98 Dodge Ram 4x4 flatbed. He also recently bought a new-to-him 2018 Jayco Jay Flight Baja Edition travel trailer. This was his first extended trip after both of these upgrades. 
Dad is largely self-employed and I have created this fundraiser to help provide him with financial stability that he needs to heal, regain his independence and resume his passion and livelihood as a Stonemason. 
Donations will be used towards these needs: 
A roof over his head to physically and emotionally recover. This may include temporary shelter and/or travel arrangements to be closer to family who can provide care and support. The ultimate goal is to eventually replace his travel trailer to ensure he has permanent shelter. 
Time away from work to heal physically and emotionally, and to ensure all medical needs are accessible to him.
A vehicle - replacing his truck with one that is capable of carrying his work tools and hauling a travel trailer is the ultimate goal. In the meantime he will need some form of transportation. 
Storage for his salvageable personal effects and undamaged work tools. 
Replacing his damaged personal effects. 
Asking for financial help is humbling and I do not take lightly making this request, especially during the instability of the current economic climate. Any amount you can donate would mean a lot. If you are unable to donate, just sharing this GoFundMe to reach more people would be helpful.
More About Alan Ash, Stonemason
What makes my dad vibrant is his passion as a Stonemason. Over the last 40 years, he has become a well-respected expert and teacher in the historical restoration and preservation of stonework. He is passionate about passing his knowledge of this dying art form on to younger generations to preserve our nation’s indigenous and modern stonework with historical accuracy. If you have been to Joshua Tree National Park, Shenandoah National Park, Lassen National Monument, Sheldon National Wildlife Refuge or Saguaro National Park you may have unknowingly seen his work and influence. He has worked on over 100 buildings on the National Register of Historic Places, within 15 Oregon State parks, at US Fish and Wildlife Service locations, on BLM historical properties and more - this list is just the tip of the iceberg. On private properties in Virginia’s Western Highlands and in Western Oregon, Dad has built hundreds of rock walls, dozens of stone chimneys and many pieces of stone art. 
Dad’s lifestyle is intensely physically active. In late 2021, one job required a daily 5-mile hike into the job site and the same hike out again at the end of a physically demanding workday. He is an incredible gardener and a lifelong musician. He is also the biggest nature lover - he regularly sends me sunset photos from incredibly remote areas.
Most importantly to me, he is the very best dad and grandpa that anyone could ask for.
I would be so thankful for any amount of money that you can donate, for sharing this fundraiser with others and also for any positive energy you can send dad’s way. 
With gratitude,
Hollie Ash

Alla and Oleksii Kryvda and their three children Nikolai (6), Sofiia (9) and Matviei (11) have finally arrived in the US after an arduous journey fleeing the war in Ukraine. They’ve lost everything and need our help to create a safe home for their family.
Before the war, the Krvyda family lived in the town of Vinnytsia, where Oleksii worked as a graphic designer and Alla worked for a bank. From the start of the war, Vinnytsia has been a Russian target. Many cruise missiles have been launched into the city, destroying the Havryshivka International Airport, the Vinnytsia TV Mast, the Ukrainian Air Force National Military Command Center, and, most tragically, the medical center, offices, stores, and civilian homes. Many citizens have lost their lives, including children, and Vinnytsia has been declared a city of war crimes.
To save their children, in early March Oleksii and Alla decided that Alla and the kids would flee to Poland via train and Oleksii would stay behind in Ukraine. They believed that the war would end and they would soon be reunited. Of course, this hope was not to be realized.
In Poland, Alla and the children were separated from Oleksii for two months. She found temporary housing, but rent prices continually increased due to the massive influx of Ukrainian refugees, so remaining in Poland was no longer a viable option. Meanwhile, Alla’s mother saw reports that the US was allowing Ukrainians fleeing the war to enter the US via Mexico. Alla learned via the internet that volunteers were meeting Ukrainians at the Tijuana airport and driving them to the US border.
The family flew to Mexico on April 24th, ready to reach a safe harbor. However, after days of grueling travel with the children, when they arrived in Tijuana on April 25th, the border had officially just closed to Ukrainians. They missed crossing into the US by three hours.
That day, the Uniting for Ukraine (U4U) refugee program was announced. Alla, Oleksii, and the children remained in Mexico for three months awaiting approval of their U4U paperwork. Speaking neither Spanish nor English, far from home and sharing a small room, they waited and hoped. On July 25th, they finally arrived at Newark Airport. Veterinarian Louise Murray and her firefighter husband, Peter, welcomed them into their home in Guilford, Connecticut, and connected them with local Ukrainian speakers who are helping the Kryvdas navigate life in the area. Their journey has been incredibly challenging physically, emotionally, and financially and the Kryvda family is still in great need of additional funding and supplies.
Oleksii is a graphic designer who needs an appropriate computer to work and support his family; the cost would be approximately $4,000. The Kryvdas also need funding to rent their own apartment or house, including at least three months’ rent to start (first month, last month, deposit). Rent in Guilford for a family of 5 is approximately $4500/month, equaling $13,500 to secure a home. The children will need clothing, shoes, winter coats, boots, and school supplies, and funds are needed for basic staples such as groceries and medical costs.
Estimated Costs:
Computer 4,000
Housing 13,500
Car insurance, maintenance, fuel 5,000
Clothes, shoes & school supplies 2,000
Food and household supplies for three months 3,000
Utilities, medical copays, and other incidentals 3,000
We hope to raise $30,000 for the Kryvda family to secure a home and care for their children for the next few months, until they are settled in and able to support themselves. Please consider a donation. The past eight months have been traumatic and frightening for the family. They are so happy to be safe and welcomed here in the US but need help getting back on their feet. No amount is too small. Thank you so much!

Their oldest son, Matt, was home during the fire and was able to call 911 and save himself and all of the family pets. Below is his message just days after the fire happened,
“Since it’s already out there, might as well just put it here, too.
This happened to me and my family. 
Just before 3pm yesterday, while home alone, I noticed smoke coming from the wall around an upstairs outlet in the corner nearest the garage. I ran downstairs to find the front of the house already fully on fire. I called 911 and got the dogs outside. By the time I got the dogs outside, the house was already filled with smoke, and I couldn’t go back in for the cats (yes, Rule #1, never re-enter a burning building, I know). My next-door neighbor, a retired firefighter, ran over before I even heard the first sirens, grabbed a garden hose, and tried to slow down the blaze until fire engines arrived. My best friend rushed over in an off-road vehicle almost at the same moment as the first fire engine pulled up. The entire neighborhood, and many of my friends, showed up while the house still burned. Once the fire was out, we saved everything we could. Firefighters found two of the cats hiding under furniture rather quickly, but Diamond and Tessa took much longer to find; thankfully, all four are alive and well.
I want to thank everyone who showed up to support my family and help salvage what we could: Danny, Trevor, and William; the Kelly, Wetzelberger, McConville, Spioch, Sisler, and Semies families; my aunts and uncles, and my cousin Devin; and so, so many more. I honestly don’t remember everyone who showed up, it was so many people. I want to thank the firefighters from all over who worked so hard to put out the blaze. And I want to thank whatever force protected my cats—and my friends for not giving up on finding Tessa when I’d abandoned hope.
I also want to thank everyone who has reached out to my family—relatives, friends, coworkers, and members of the community—to offer help and support. Right now, we are still processing, still taking stock, and still figuring out what’s next. In the days and months to come, we will have better answers to everyone who has asked what they can do to help us. We appreciate it immensely, but right now, 34 hours later, I still don’t have a good answer. But thank you so, so much, from the bottom of my heart, just for being there.
This is a devastating loss, but it could have been so much worse. I am alive. My dogs and cats are alive. We saved far more than any of us expected. That’s what matters most.
So, um, yeah. I don’t know what else to say. I don’t know what’s next. We’re going through the unimaginable. Just … thank you.”

Please help us share sweet Beckham's story and help Nick, Angela, & Brooks during this time of unimaginable heartache. Thank you for your prayers and support during this time.
Beckhams' story from his Momma:
Beckham Nicholas Peterson 
October 26th 2022
6 lbs 13oz 20.5 inches long 
Beckham went home to be with our Heavenly Father Saturday, November 12th.
While we are broken into a million pieces, we want to share Beckham's story as we know he has so many people lifting him in prayer and love him so deeply. Even though his time on earth was very short, he is truly the most special, little boy. 
After an ultrasound growth scan on August 31st, our OB saw something concerning and referred us to a specialist at Maternal Fetal Medicine in Columbia.  On September 9th, It was there we were told that something was very wrong with Beckham.  The doctor there diagnosed that at some point he had an aneurysm and was missing portions of his brain.  She was concerned that he would pass in utero, likely within days.  Shocked and absolutely devastated, and obviously confused as Beckham was reacting to sounds and had full movement of his limbs, we decided to go to Children's Hospital in St. Louis for a second opinion. The following Monday at Children's hospital, they confirmed our greatest fears, that something was very wrong with him and he needed to be monitored very closely.  Beckham was originally diagnosed with arteriovenous malformation (AVM) and Vein of Galen Malformation.  The nuero team later deemed Beckham had multiple large AVMs within his brain, operable but still very concerning. AVM is an abnormal tangle of blood vessels connecting arteries and veins, which disrupts normal blood flow to and from the heart.  Due to the AVM, Beckham was already showing cardiac failure.  His heart was twice as large as it should be and an echocardiogram showed fluid building throughout his body and organs, aka hydrops fetalis.  Doctors were uncertain of what this really meant for him, not knowing if intervention was a possibility. If so, his body would grow around his heart and would basically correct itself. It was there they made a plan, the team of cardiologists, MFMs, and Neurosurgeons wanted to see Beckham weekly to monitor his heart failure and the AVM.  Another risk was for myself.  The doctors were concerned that I could develop mirror syndrome.  Basically, my body would start to mirror what was happening inside Beckham's body.  Beginning that week, Nick and I made weekly trips to St. Louis and Columbia to monitor myself and Beckham.  Week by week, Beckham continued to hang on and somewhat improved.  The fluid around his organs decreased and Beckham was growing at a normal rate.  There was concern of me being able to carry until full term since there were multiple complications. Doctors were unsure if he would be stillborn or if he could survive birth. Once he was disconnected from me, would he be able to function on his own?  We had a million unknowns but held onto hope because we knew we were in the best hands and ultimately we knew that the outcome of this wasn't up to us, it was all in God's hands. The emotional ups and downs that came with this were filled with heartbreak and hope. Praying so hard. Our God is a God of miracles.  Begging Him for that miracle until the very last second.
The doctors had a planned induction on October 31st, we had made it to 37 weeks and defying all the odds, Beckham was an active boy in utero, stable and still fighting.  Well, Beckham had his own plans and decided that October 26th was a better time for him. After going to a local hospital our team of doctors in St. Louis didn't want to risk him being born in Columbia away from their team.  After a short helicopter ride later, we had made it to Children's for the birth. After a fairly quick labor and delivery, he was born - alive! They took him right away to the NICU to assess him and see what kind of help he needed. To their surprise they were over prepared for our little fighter. We had even more hope that he was going to be okay. After a few days of testing and scans, the news came. Beckham's AVM was inoperable. There was nothing they could do for him. Hearing this news along with, "Im so sorry but this is one in a million" was our biggest fear in the whole 9 week process.
Why him, he did nothing to deserve this. Why us? Why choose our sweet Beckham to be that one in a million? Something we will never understand. 
We were given the gift of 17 really precious days with him. Snuggling him as best we could, talking to him and telling him stories about his family, reading books, singing lullabies, telling him how much we love him, meeting so many friends and family and oh so many kisses. 
One of Beckhams favorite things was hearing our voices, especially his daddy’s.  He would look all around to find him when he heard his voice. 
This process has led us to meet so many incredible people, including the doctors and nurses at Children's and BJC, with the biggest hearts that we will never forget.  
Thank you for all of the love, prayers and support that we have been surrounded with during this unimaginable time. 
We pray that Beckham is forever remembered by so many and he will always have a very big piece of our hearts. Forever our little boy. Our Fighter.

Our mom, Robin Walsh, loved nature and being outdoors. She raised us in a home on the edge of a forest by a stream, and our happiest memories are there with her. We breathed in the Arboretum's scented lilacs on Mother's Day weekends. We enjoyed sunsets over Peter's Hill, eyes on our Boston skyline. We brought the littlest ones to the waterfalls and taught them the secret paths Mom had helped us find.
When she had to leave us earlier this week, we knew we wanted to honor her life in a way that would've brought her joy and comfort. We are hoping to gather donations towards the purchase of a bench at the Arnold Arboretum in her honor. All money raised will benefit the Arboretum's preservation and cultivation of its magnificent landscape that our mom loved so dearly.
Purchasing a bench in our mother's honor costs $10,000. Any donation toward this goal is deeply appreciated.

While she was at JCU, she was Chapter President of her sorority, Kappa Delta in 2012 and Vice-President of Operations in 2011. She was also a member of the Order of Omega Pi Sigma Alpha Honors Program. She earned her Juris Doctorate from Cleveland Marshall School of Law in 2016 where she was a student clinician with the Cleveland Marshall Advocacy Clinic, and a member of the Women's Law Student Association.
On May 21, 2021, she married the love of her life, Matt Keene, whom she had been together with for 8 years. Alyssa and Matt spent the majority of their loving and strong relationship all over the Cleveland area; from their favorite hangout spot of choice Angelo's Pizza, next door to their Lakewood apartments, to just enjoying spending time with one another in their brand-new home in Willowick. Avid Vegas travelers, Alyssa loved to enjoy those bright lights and fancy hotels and making sure she got those high roller chips away from Matt at the Roulette tables.

Dreams of having a large family, their eight-month-old son Ryan Patrick Keene came along and changed Alyssa's heart forever. She was an amazing mother and wife. She began her career at Ritzler, Coughlin, and Paglia, LTD as a law clerk and moved to an attorney after passing the Bar exam. Alyssa had some day hoped to serve on the Supreme Court. Alyssa was a member of the Cleveland Metropolitan Bar Association. Alyssa was currently employed with Gallagher Sharp in Cleveland.

Dear family and friends,
Our hearts are heavy and our lives are forever altered. On October 19, our bashful, selfless, brilliant and extraordinarily sweet Tyler passed away unexpectedly at the age of 22. Possessing a larger-than-life spirit, accompanied by a kind and humble demeanor, Tyler was an absolute blessing to all who knew him. Whether it was his plants, his two pugs, or his beloved little sister, he was always nurturing something or someone. Tyler truly enjoyed the simple things in life. He enjoyed pretty things...things that tasted good, sounded good, and smelled good. He’d see something lovely and go, “Ooooooh!!!” He’d pick up a candle and go, “Mmmmmmm.” A sandy beach, the vast ocean, a koi pond, beautiful garden or specialty coffee shop were his go-tos. His gentle nature did not tolerate conflict well. I’ve never seen him angry. When upset, he would say, “It kinda made me mad” in a very calm, far-from-mad voice. He appreciated a pleasant and uncomplicated lifestyle. Our Ty lived very simply, but his mind was an intricate network of intrigue and wonderment! He pursued his interests until he became a subject matter expert, quietly conquering one challenge after the next. He had a flare for the Japanese culture so much that he wanted his genealogy test to reflect that he was at least 1% Asian. Although born and primarily raised in Montana, 'The Salt Life" beckoned him. He moved to San Diego, California with his family where he lived until his passing. Tyler was gifted in so many ways, evidenced by his ability to play several instruments, perform complex pieces on the violin, grow exotic plants, and draw intricately...no words can do him justice!
In the spirit of transparency, we desperately await answers but suspect a misdiagnosis that may have taken him from us unnecessarily. I feel that it’s only fair to Ty that we say that out loud and cope with that possibility. He became ill in May and fought bravely but in true Ty fashion, very politely, for his life. He was able to identify and clearly articulate his declining health, but it fell on deaf ears. My sister did everything she could to advocate for and save her son. That battle included some substantial expenses.
As we grasp for answers and cling tightly to God’s promises, we must also begin the difficult task of making preparations to celebrate a life well lived but taken far too soon. We know that many hands make light work so, we humbly come before you to ask for your assistance in covering the expenses associated with such a tragedy as this. We hope to cover funeral expenses, assist with last-minute travel costs, and recover some out-of-pocket medical expenses.
For those of you who knew Ty personally and loved him endlessly...thank you!
Although there is a permanent vacancy in our hearts, we are lifted up by your love and encouraged by the hope we have in a future with our Father in Heaven. We will be reunited...oh what a day of rejoicing that will be!

Full back story (scroll to the bottom for a summary):
Back in 2008, my little sister was born. She was born at 26 weeks, weighing in at 2 lbs 3 oz. At the same time, my parents were losing pay and benefits because of the 2008 housing crash. My dad's paychecks began getting garnished, debt collectors harassed us every day, and my parents ultimately had their house foreclosed on.
Just before the bank took the house, my parents were scrambling to find us a new place to live. They had zero credit, little money, and two children to take care of. One day, my dad was able to find a place. The landlady of the home talked to my dad, and she recognized our last name: Hollenback. She said that my dad's great-grandmother was the first female doctor in Brevard County and took good care of her. So, she made my dad a deal. She would rent us a 3 bed, 2 bath house just on the county border for $950/month. So, we moved in immediately, just before the bank placed a large lock on our old home's front door. Keep in mind, it's 2008, so price for rent was nothing like it is today (and wages have stayed the same).
Fast forward a few years, our land lady passes away. We discovered that, in her will, she wished that the rent would not be raised on my parents. So, for 12 years, they've lived in that house for $950/month. My parents have been barely getting by this whole time, as both have working-class jobs and no college education. On top of that, we always have car troubles, so a lot of money goes into repairs for the cars and appliances in the home.
Now, there is a new landlord, and she's decided that she is going to sell the house. They were told to be out by December 1st. Now that the housing market is completely wild in my hometown (Cocoa, FL), the average price to rent a 2 bed 1 bath apartment is at least $1600.

I am so afraid of my family becoming houseless, and I don't want that for my parents, who have worked so hard their whole life... and I DEFINITELY don't want my little sister (she's 14) to go through that.
So, I've laid it all out and I am so appreciative if you have taken the time to read my family's story. Please, if you can, share this with your network, with your friends, family, etc. Every single penny is appreciated and will go toward moving costs and rent for the first couple of months so my parents can get on their feet after landing in a new living situation.
Thank you so so much for your time.

This is a story of how I met Kim and hope to help her out of homelessness. She needs a little support for a few months while she waits for government assistance. If Kim can get support, she might be able to start again. She's a very kind person who takes care of other homeless in the area. She also dreams of opening a homeless shelter one day. I hope you can support her during this rough time. In shaa Allah. A little bit of kindness goes a long way!
I met Kim in front of a shopping center. She looked tired, pushing herself in her wheelchair across the parking lot. I looked at her, and she smiled at me with a wonderful smile. Then she complimented me. I remember she said, “You look pretty.”  
“Thank you,” I replied.  “You too!”
It felt genuine. I asked her if she needed some help getting around. She thanked me, and I pushed her a few steps when she said I could go. I refused, in a polite way, trying to complete my mini mission. I wanted to help her get to her destination. She thanked me again, and I kept pushing her along. 
Finally, when we reached the end of the sidewalk, she told me I could go again. I refused again, thinking the stop was some store nearby. She paused and said she had a confession to make. Kim wasn’t trying to go to a store nearby. Kim was trying to hold up a sign. She wanted to go to the highway to hold up a small green sign. I had a feeling. I did. But I kept telling myself, praying inside, that Kim wasn’t homeless. 
I know we’ve seen it many times before. The highway sign holders. It takes a lot of cold blood to drive past people who are just like us but have been dealt different circumstances, yet we do it all the time. I guess the biggest issue that goes through our mind is “what can I possibly do to help?” Even if I did give them the extra cash I have in the cupholder in my car, what difference does that make? And so we see them, but we don’t. We really don’t. 
I stopped pushing the wheelchair. I didn’t know what to do, so I just placed my hand on her head and gave her a sort of hug. Kim cried. And I felt I had reached into the realm many, many exist in. A realm we’ve blinded ourselves to. I had never truly felt a homeless person cry. It became so real I could not ignore it. 
I moved in front of Kim, and I told her I was sorry. I was sorry and this situation should not have been the case for her. She told me that she had been homeless after moving out from a family member's place, where the living situation became very dangerous. Kim has lupus and a combination of other health issues that require her to use a wheelchair to move around. She also needs a lot of medical care and says she is eligible for 30 hours a week of home healthcare, which she has a very hard time receiving. Due to her disabilities, Kim can’t get a blue-collar job, and without a job, it's kind of hard to get out of homelessness. 
I asked Kim about any organizations she had tried reaching out to; did she apply for section 8 housing? Did she look for homeless shelters that could help her out?  Kim replied that there is only so much organizations can do to help. She explained that they assist with basic necessities like food, water, and new clothes. This can be really helpful; however, the effect is limited. 
Not only that, Kim explained that homeless shelters are often filled to capacity and can also be extremely dangerous. An NPR interview titled Why Some Homeless Choose The Streets Over Shelters explained that lots of people feel more comfortable on the streets than in many shelters because of this. As for section 8 housing, she’s on the waitlist; however, the waitlist can take up to 18 months, according to Kim, and even two years, according to eligibility.com, a website that explains eligibility requirements for government programs.
This is not ideal. Along with inflation, increasing rent, and Kim’s unemployment, it's a real struggle to just get by day to day. Currently, Kim is staying in a motel, raising money on the highway to keep this temporary shelter. What's more, Kim explained to me that she isn’t the sole profiter from the money she raises. She makes it a point to donate what she can afford to other homeless people she knows. 
Kim explained how frustrated she feels about the stereotypes of the homeless, ideas that often dehumanize and blame normal people for financial issues they could not have anticipated. This idea that has seeped into our worldview makes people feel invisible. She made me face what I already knew;  Kim used a word our hyper-individualistic American culture often refuses to admit influences our lives, “Circumstance.”
It could have been any of us. According to World Population Review, there are over half a million homeless people in the U.S., Texas being number 4 on the list of the most homeless in America. With these numbers, it's difficult to imagine how we can blame all those people for being at fault for their situation.

Where were you Sunday afternoon? Many of us are fortunate enough to be with family, resting, or enjoying Sunday football. Most New Orleanians on October 9th were watching Taysom Hill make 4 touch downs as the Saints beat the Seahawks.
Survivor “X” was working. At 1:15pm, she was sweeping a client’s front porch when a man approached. Politely declining the conversation, she turned to go back inside. It is then the man went onto the porch and aggressively pushed her inside the house. “X” was brutally attacked in the hall, and the man attempted to rape her. “X” fought. She fought hard, being punched and bitten, but she was able to prevent the rape. Screaming and pleading for her life, the man grew more angry. He wrapped his hands around her neck, squeezing hard in attempt to take her last breath. He is still at large.
“X” survived, but she is left with a badly beaten body, and even worse, severe mental and psychological trauma. Dark bruises remain on her chest and throat, and she has difficulty speaking and eating. Her food is thinned. Her hands are severely swollen and she can’t hold things. She has stitches, bruises and contusions all over her body. She is scared to leave her home, or open the door. She can not work. To feel safe, family and friends stay with her. She has good days and some really bad days. Her memories come and go, and she fights every minute of every day to stay in the now, and look to the future.
Our names are Katherine Sauska and Sarah Hillery, and “X” is a great friend. We have independently known her nearly fifteen years each. She has helped us in our homes, with our children, and is there for us even when we don't know we need her. Her daughter is friends with our daughters. She, and her family, have become our family, and she is a woman we trust more than almost anyone. We want to help “X” as she has helped us and so many others.
“X” is a woman of faith, family, friendship and service. She is honest, kind, and the epitome of integrity. She puts the needs of others in front her own, so much so she works every day to provide for her family and the community she serves. Even on Sundays.
A mother of two daughters (one still living at home), a wife, and a grandmother, “X” needs our help. While we continue to search for this violent, dangerous man, in a time with little police resources and political chaos, “X” and her family are suffering. Unable to work, her bills will go unpaid. Unable to use her hands, she can’t cook meals or care for her home and family. Medical bills from this horrific event will not be small. She needs help getting her daughter to school. More than that, she and her family need therapy to get through this traumatic event. The time it will take to recover is unknown. While the physical wounds disappear, survivors of this kind of trauma will experience weeks, months and even years of mental anguish, especially without the economic means to get therapy and to take the time needed to heal. Knowing the man is still out there only makes it worse.
This go fund me is for her. The funds will be used entirely to help “X” and her family get through this event. It will be used to help alleviate the financial stress of daily bills, meals, transportation, chores, medical bills and to provide therapy for she and her family.
Rape survivors often struggle with guilt and shame preventing them to share their stories. “X” dealt with her own version of these feelings, but as we rally around her, she has agreed to share her story publicly. She has even agreed to use her name, but per advise from officers we have hidden her name. Being the beautiful soul she is, she wants to do so to help other women. She wants women to know they must be safe. She wants them to know that a busy street, or a nice neighborhood, or the time of day doesn’t make you safe. We must keep guard, always. If sharing her story can help others, and we in turn can help her, perhaps we all can make the world a little bit better.
Please consider helping “X”, her family, and all the lives she touches. Every little bit helps.

The details of the long version, or at least variants thereof, are likely familiar to many of you. My wife and I are fighting to keep our heads above the proverbial water from month to month. Of the two of us, I'm the only one who is gainfully employed, with all but perhaps a handful of my wife's 100+ applications over the past half a year going unanswered. Then, even if someone did return her calls and hire her, my wife deals with chronic pain that would make holding many jobs difficult. Even standing for longer than a half hour is trying for her joints, and disability really isn't an option with how much it costs to get the diagnoses and such required to prove a case. And while my physical health is relatively stable, I have been noticing more and more lately that my mental health is wavering, to the point where I've seen it impacting my work. I genuinely fear for the moment it passes beyond a stage that allows me to 'fake it,' as it were.
As it stands, we are behind by more than two payments on most bills, mortgage chief among them, and facing our third shutoff notice for our electricity in as many months. Our trash service has also been suspended until we are caught up on payments. I have been doing my best to play catch-up where I can, but it honestly isn't enough, and dipping the account into the red over and over only makes things worse. Suddenly that $20 you put in the tank becomes $56 from an overdraft fee because other payments came out when they shouldn't have. Being forced to sell our home and beg relatives for a room is creeping closer and closer to being our next move, but even that has its hurdles and offers no guarantees.
I've set the goal at a total that represents the ideal (catch up on bills, knock out some of the recurring debt), though I don't expect to get anywhere near that. The minimum amount that would let us survive without my losing my sanity any faster than I am is about 4K or so. But as we all know, that kind of thing fluctuates rather quickly, even from week to week, so I don't know how long those numbers will remain accurate before they would need to increase to be sufficient.
So here I am, asking whoever is reading this mess to please help if it within your means. Every little bit will help. I'm used to being the one that gives to these kinds of drives, so it feels very strange and out of place to now be the one asking for help.
I thank everyone in advance for taking the time to read this, and for doing what you can to give and/or spread the word. Truly, thank you.

Experience with large breed dogs and following through on continued training is a requirement. 2 lessons with their current trainer is included. 
Any amount donated towards their training would be greatly appreciated. If interested in adopting, please express interest in messages.

It has always been my passion to work with wildlife. Since graduating in 2017 from the University of Vermont with a Bachelor of Science in Wildlife & Fisheries Biology, I have had the opportunity to live and work in 8 states as a wildlife technician on different projects. I learned early on in my career that I wanted to work with lesser-known species of conservation concern.
It was with great excitement that I started graduate school at Antioch University New England in 2020, pursuing a Master of Science in Environmental Studies with a Conservation Biology concentration. While pursuing my degree, I began my thesis study on a bird in my home state of Massachusetts, the Brown Thrasher! While not as well studied as other birds in the region, the Brown Thrasher is just as important! My study aims to determine if the Brown Thrasher has a preferred habitat in Massachusetts. I have had great success researching this bird the past two summers! Once completed, my thesis will be published through Antioch University New England and sent to Massachusetts Fish & Wildlife to help implement conservation and management practices for the Brown Thrasher.
The summer of 2023 will be my final field season studying the Brown Thrasher before I begin my data analysis. The data collection takes place in shrubland adjacent to different habitats (farmland, pine barren forests, and deciduous forests) and the shrubby edges of farmland. During early spring, I conduct point counts from sunrise to 9 am and record all birds I see and hear. While the emphasis is on the Brown Thrasher, it is important to document all birds detected in these areas for further analysis. Later in the summer, I return to each field site to collect vegetation data for habitat analysis; this consists of but is not limited to measuring vegetation height, identifying plant species, and measuring downed woody debris.
I have applied to a few small grants, but funding has been limited! This summer, my field sites are in Western Massachusetts. I am looking for funding for housing ($700), partial tuition payment for thesis credits during the summer ($1,300), and gas reimbursement ($500). Any additional funding would go towards the remaining tuition costs for my final year in grad school! Please see below for more information regarding the Brown Thrasher.
Thank you so much!
Alec Woolf
In the Northeastern United States, birds residing in shrubland and early-successional habitats are a guild that is declining due to habitat loss in the region (King and Schlossberg 2014). Since 1950, New England has lost 66 percent of its shrubland habitat (King and Schlossberg 2014). Currently, powerline corridors provide roughly 10 percent of shrubland habitat for species in Massachusetts (King et al. 2014).
One shrubland avian species that is declining in the northeast is the Brown Thrasher (Toxostoma rufum). The Brown Thrasher can be found from the Northeastern United States to just east of the Rocky Mountains and parts of Texas. In the Northeast, the Brown Thrasher’s decline tends to vary from state to state. Based on breeding bird surveys, the Brown Thrasher has declined from 25-45 %. It is considered a species of conservation concern in several states, such as New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, Vermont, and New Jersey. In Massachusetts specifically, the Brown Thrasher has declined by 32 %. The Brown Thrasher has mainly disappeared from the Southeastern and Western parts of Massachusetts (Mass Audubon 2022).
In the Northeast, the Brown Thrasher is found in shrubby fields with young trees, powerline areas, and pine barrens (Cavitt, J. F. and C. A. Haa 2020; NH Fish & Game, n.d). Due to its cryptic nature, the Brown Thrasher's migration patterns are not well known, especially its fall migration. Thrashers are known to arrive in Massachusetts in mid to late April. Based on spring 2017-2022 findings, birders have detected Brown Thrashers along the coast, on farmland, within pine barren conservation areas, and near hardwood forests (E-Bird 2022).
