The Story:
On September 29, our friend Mo launched his 1968 wood troller, Galaxy from Boat Haven in Port Townsend. Mo has lived aboard Galaxy for seven years, and had just spent the summer hauled-out in the shipyard working on some projects that included repairs in the plywood deck, rebedding hardware, bottom paint, and most importantly a new paint job on the hull. Upon launch Galaxy took on water, as wood boats are expected to do, and Mo waited until she took up and the water slowed to a trickle before heading off. About a mile from the marina, Mo noticed that Galaxy had become bow down, with water trapped behind the forward-most bulkhead. Unfortunately it was already too late. Water began flooding in through seams in the top side of the hull that were still open. The pumps were not keeping up, water was rising above the cabin floor, and Mo made the necessary decision to alert the Coast Guard, who rescued Mo, and called in a tow boat to save Galaxy. Within several hours, Mo was dropped off by the tow boat back at Boat Haven, and Galaxy, who'd become submerged above the cabin top, was turned upright and hoisted into the Travelift by the skilled Boat Haven operators during an emergency haul-out in the middle of the night. Galaxy stayed in the travelift slings overnight draining, while friends surrounded Mo for support, food, accommodations, and love. Galaxy was blocked back up in the shipyard in the morning and Mo got right to work, surveying the damage, pumping out the bilge, cleaning up, and salvaging as much as possible.
A Little About Mo:
Mo is one of the kindest, gentlest, most generous people I've ever met. I first met Mo at the Northwest School of Wooden Boatbuilding, where I was a student and where he works. Mo has attended both the Wooden Boat Building program and the Marine Systems program, and has become a highly knowledgeable and skilled shipwright and systems technician. Mo's patience, warmth, and willingness to always help are just some of the characteristics that his friends love him for, and what makes him a particularly important member of the community both at the school and in the larger Port Townsend area. Mo is an avid sailor and outdoors person; he enjoys exploring the Salish Sea and Puget Sound along with Mt. Rainer, the Cascades, and the Olympics.
The Good:
Galaxy's engine is a Detroit Diesel, and Mo reached out to Walt Trisdale, Port Townsend's renowned diesel engine expert who shared several strategies to dry out and revive the engine. Mo followed Walt's protocol and in a giant win, fired up the engine on October 4th. Luckily Mo has also been able to salvage and clean some of his essential belongings, including clothing, kitchenware, some books, and non-power tools.
The Not-So-Good:
All of the electronics aboard Galaxy are destroyed, including multiple battery banks, chargers, inverter, GPS, chart plotter, depth sounder, engine gauges, cameras (film and digital), and laptop. The wiring will all need to be torn out and replaced. All of Mo's power tools are also destroyed, despite an attempt to de-salt them. Nearly everything on board Galaxy that made her a home; books, bedding, and cushions have been destroyed. Aside from the expenses that come with replacing items, Mo is also facing a $20,000 tow boat bill, along with Boat Haven's emergency haulout fees, and additional unanticipated shipyard fees. The good news is that Mo has an insurance policy for Galaxy which will cover the cost of the salvage operation and at least some of the destroyed equipment.
What We're Hoping For:
We're launching this fundraiser at $10,000, all of which will be used to cover the replacement of Galaxy's electronics, Mo's tools, personal belongings, emergency haulout fees, shipyard fees, and ongoing living expenses as Mo continues to clean Galaxy up and restore her to her former glory, so that he can continue living aboard and caring for this sweet boat.
Wood Boats and Their Caretakers:
Wood boats are one of the things that Port Townsend is famous for, and are known for the unique processes required to build them and the craftsmanship that is needed to maintain them. Owners of wood boats see a beauty and a soul in them that is different from other types of hulls. Most boat owners shy away from wood, claiming it is a needy type of boat, but wood boat owners claim their wood boats give back exponentially. A few wood boats continue to be built today, but it takes a special type of person to care for and maintain these sweet relics of the past. Mo is committed to being one of the wood boat caretakers, and he wants to give Galaxy the love and attention she deserves.

TL:DR: My sweet sister kitties that I adopted through the Feline Rescue Association ate a lily that came in my boque of flowers for my birthday from Baltimore's Florist that was not the bouquet my friend ordered :( (it was not supposed to have Lillies in them)
They spent the weekend in the Emergeny Vet and hit me with a big financial strain. They are home and doing well now thank goodness! Any help would be appreciated! See below to read more about our story!
Hi my name is Alissa and I’m the proud cat mom of the two cuties Poe and Riley above. I was fortunate and blessed to adopt them from the Feline Rescue Association last October. They are sisters and the sweetest girls, they are inseparable and are each other's Ying to their Yang. As you can see in the photos below Poe has all the sass in speaking her mind and loves to comment on my decorations. Riley is a calm and brings all the zen vibes. They spend the day cuddling each other and each one sleeps on both sides of me at night by my head (of course Riley needs to be under the covers ). They really are truly my children!
Last Wednesday was my 30th birthday and my best friend who recently moved two hours away sent flowers to my job from the company Baltimore's Florist. Unfortunately it was not the bouquet she ordered and they didn’t inform her of the change, she is aware Lillie’s are toxic to cats. I was so excited that day I didn’t realize there were two Lillie’s in the bouquet and they weren’t bloomed yet (I ALWAYS CHECK ). On Friday morning I woke up to my worst nightmare. They were throwing up and I didn’t see which one or if both, and there was a half eaten Lilly on the floor. I went into panic mode of course.
My neighbor called poison control line for me as I had to run out to meet my boss for a conference meeting and her and my mom managed to get them into the crates and to the emergency vet asap (it truly takes a village and I’m so grateful for mine!)
As all of this is happening, my friend contacted the flower shop and spoke with the executive director who informed her this should not have happened and any changes needed to be approved by the person who purchased them. She attempted to contact the direct flower store to find out what kind of lily it was and they REFUSED and said they could not disclose that information! (In an animal emergency that it’s imperative information!!! This isn’t HIPPA of the flowers!) The executive director was unsuccessful in follow up conversations with them and is now looking into things herself for the sequence of unacceptable events.
My mom resides in Bowie and took them to cats and dogs. After being told it would be $6,600 on top of the $1.200 they had already charged I was devastated. I could only think the worst was to come already knowing how toxic it is, the thought of loosing them or having to surrender because of these numbers made me fall to the ground. Only to then find out they had not started any treatment even though they had been there for 6.5 hours knowing how time sensitive treatment is and already have gotten permission to start treatment.
My mom and I rushed them to Emergency Animal Hospital of Ellicott City and I am so thankful we did as they took exceptional care of them and the charges were not as high! I felt confident that they were in good hands with them and they would do everything they could.
They finally came back home to me last night and just had their 24 hour visit follow up and all labs are normal!
I am beyond thankful that they are home and healthy (and now I’m an official paranoid helicopter mom even more than before) I never thought I would be in a place to need to create a go fund me but this has been a serious strain on my finances and my mom who also helped me. I (as I always jokingly but in truth say) live independently on a social work salary .
There was no way I wasn’t going to figure something out for them and not have them treated due to this but I never imagined we’d be here. I know emergency vets are expensive but MAN, was I truly shocked-this was one of my worst fears and I just again never imagined something like this to happen. I know I felt immense guilt for not noticing it (too much excitement from the birthday I guess UGH) and my friend felt such guilt for what happened. But accidents unfortunately do happen.
Poe, Riley and I would appreciate any help that anyone could give to us. They truly are my world and have given more to me than I could ever give to them. They have given me feelings of purpose, joy and have been there to lift me up in hard times and they will never know how much they bring to me!

How Beth, The Fairy CatMother gave Rutherford a home
During COVID, Beth started fostering cats. She nicknamed herself “The Fairy CatMother,” because she said, “my job is to take these cats in and clean them up, give them somewhere safe to hang out, and help them get dressed up for the ball to find their forever homes.”
In April 2021, Beth began to foster Rutherford, the sweetest friendliest kitty in the Cativerse. The rescue estimated him to be about 2 years old. He won her heart right away as an unusually doglike cat with an adorable face that has been described as looking like he was caught eating a jar of peanut butter. He is the rare magical cat that kisses strangers to greet them, actually likes belly rubs, and politely gazes up at visitors asking if he can sit in their lap.
As time passed, Beth and Rutherford developed a unique bond. Beth realized she didn’t want to let him go. There was just one problem: Rutherford had been diagnosed with a rare, fatal congenital heart defect. On average, cats with this type of diagnosis live 6–18 months.
Heart Trouble in Catland
Part of Rutherford's heart is growing the wrong way, causing it to be unable to work as well as normal. This leads to congestive heart failure, where fluid builds up in the chest surrounding the lungs. The condition is fatal. The question is when? It could be a month, or perhaps a few years if he’s very lucky. Getting his treatment right has been a high-wire balancing act between Beth and his University of Minnesota Cardiology team. They need to give enough medicine to reduce the fluid around his lungs so he can breathe, but not so much that it damages his kidneys. Repeated chest taps (manually removing the fluid around his lungs with a needle), heart scans, and other procedures to find out what's going on, without giving him trauma.
﻿But if you know Beth, you know that there's no one else in the world who will work harder to make sure he gets everything he needs.
Hope for Rutherford
His veterinarians all agree that Beth's care has extended Rutherford's life and continues to make it a good one. At some point, she will likely have to make a heart-wrenching decision about his quality of life; the most likely end for him is suffering from fluid buildup that they can’t control, or suffering from kidney damage caused by his medications. But Beth doesn't want to make that decision based on the cost of Rutherford’s care. Not before he's ready. His life is filled with love, snuggles, friends, neighbors, and cat tv looking out windows at trees full of birds and squirrels, and yard theater watching all the bunnies and critters a kitty could over dream of from the safety of his kennel.
How to help Rutherford
The cost up to now finding the right balance in his treatment is a lot for a Fairy CatMother to handle. This is a preexisting condition, so pet insurance isn't an option. In the year since his adoption, Rutherford's heart-related medical needs have cost nearly $7,000. And it's not over yet. More scans and tests will be needed as his vets continue to evaluate the best way to care for him, and he is likely to need more chest taps when his disease progresses.
To that end, Rutherford and Beth are looking for some support from their community. They are so thankful and appreciate all support, including any amount of donation, sharing of this fundraiser with other people, and your prayers and good thoughts.
Here are some approximations of costs until now, just to give you an idea.
$800–$1200: Emergency room visits for dangerous declines
$450: Echocardiogram/heart scans to check on his condition
$400: Chest taps to remove fluid from around his lungs
$200: Check-ups to make sure medications aren’t damaging his organs
$130: Five kinds of medicine (monthly)
$50: Appetite stimulant to counteract medication (monthly)

Our hearts are heavy to announce that our dad, William “Bill” Snead of Hialeah, Florida, born on December 28th, 1951 in Stone Mountain, Georgia, peacefully passed away at age 70 on November 9th, 2022 in Duluth, Georgia. 
While unexpected, we are grateful to know that our dad left this world laughing, joking, and surrounded by love and family. We miss him more every day, wishing we could hear the same ol’ jokes just one more time.
For those that have not had a chance to meet him, to know one of his children is to know him. For we carry with us his quirks, his legacies, and memories that narrate what a wonderful father he was to five children.
Bill had a humble and caring servant’s heart and shared what he could to assist others.  He volunteered his time and energy to help his friends and his community and even devoted time as a volunteer firefighter.  He followed his father’s and older brothers’ footsteps, and in showing his love for his country, proudly served in the United States Army for over 20 years.  He began his career as a Cannon Crewmember and then moved into the occupational specialty of Satellite Communication Systems Operator-Maintainer, and retired as a Staff Sergeant in 1993 out of Fort Gordon, Georgia.  During his time of service, he was able to travel the world and appreciate God’s creations.
After the Army, Bill worked hard for his family and provided them with love, support, and strength.  He was a free spirit, and encouraged his children to live their own dreams and destinies.  His biggest wish was for his family to be happy and to thrive as their genuine selves, and to never hurt or take advantage of others.  Bill cherished his wife, Suki, and they were best friends for over 45 years.  They loved making memories together, whether it was traveling, watching Korean soap operas, drinking coffee in peace, sharing stories and making jokes, and watching their children successfully navigate their own way through the world.
Bill lit up the room when he walked in, as he was a giant of a man with an even bigger personality.  He was a jokester and used his humor to make people laugh and feel at ease. With his insight and wisdom, he gave others a safe space to be comfortable.  He told entertaining stories and would always made time to listen to what others had to say. Bill was a beautiful person to be around. Bill lived a life following his passions and shared those talents with people who were in his life. You would often see him crafting cigar boxes guitars and ukuleles; carving wood into novelty toys and pieces of art; or writing short stories or poetry. As family was fundamentally important to him, he researched the Snead family genealogy, making connections and assisting others with finding more about their own family history.  He also enjoyed listening to music, reading his bible before bed, and keeping in touch with friends and family.
We are so humbled and grateful for all the people that have reached out to share their support and memories of our dad. Every day we are reminded of how wonderful our dad was, to have impacted so many.
Based on our father’s wishes, his surviving five children and grandchildren are gathering from all over the world to meet at our mother’s house in Georgia, and then we will caravan to dad’s hometown of Hialeah, Florida to honor him in a memorial service on 22 November.
Dad always expressed of wanting to go on an “epic road trip” with his family in tow. As a tribute to our father, we will use part of the proceeds to help fund the caravan down to Florida, cover memorial service costs, and the remaining funds will be used to take care of our dad’s best friend, our mother. Perhaps sensing his time, our dad made us promise that we would do our best to take care of our mom- showing his immense love and dedication to her.

Meet our little boy, Jasper—a Costa Rican kitty who was rescued at the age of approximately, 4-weeks old, in April 2022, from Puerto Viejo, Limon, Costa Rica. He’s been blessed with a beautiful life here in Toronto, Canada— with family and friends who love him. 
If you’ve had the opportunity to meet Jasper, you know he’s the most curious and playful kitty there is. Much like a Dog, he loves to cuddle throughout the night into the early AM and you can depend on him to bring light to your day and a smile to your face, no matter how busy or overwhelmed you are. His spunky and charismatic personality always keeps us laughing. He is a source of pure love and joy and is always looking for the next kiss. He loves human interaction and especially enjoys playing with his feline neighbours—whom he calls out to on our balcony throughout the day.
On Wednesday, October 18th, we noticed unusual behaviour from Jasper—he wasn’t himself, he was squatting all over the house, trying to pee, but nothing would come out. He was crying in pain, like we’ve never heard before. When you tried to comfort him, he would scream. There was vomit on the floor and his food/water was left untouched. His bladder was firm and unexpressable. He walked himself to the dark washroom and rested on the rug. We immediately took him to the local veterinary emergency clinic and on a worst come, first serve basis—they declared it an urgent, life-threatening emergency. 
The doctor examined him and shortly after, diagnosed him with a Urethral obstruction, which is very unusual for a kitten his age. This is a life-threatening condition that requires immediate attention. A urinary catheter was used to resolve the obstruction (that felt like gritty sand material) and allow urine to flow again. Although Jasper was extremely dehydrated, his electrolyte levels looked fine and he was given medication in hospital. An abdominal x-ray did not show evidence of bladder stones. However, there are stones that are not visible on x-ray (only ultrasound). A urinalysis and blood test was submitted and results were pending—Jasper was sent home later that night and was declared an outpatient with careful monitoring at home.
The moment he got home, he ran to his water bowl and drank like he’s never seen water before. We then comforted him in our arms as he closed his eyes and purred. Eventually, he made his way to his litter and stood there for hours, struggling to pee, until he eventually fell asleep. We took him to his bed, but he persisted and made his way back to the litter. Confused and still unable to pee, we found him sleeping in his litter that morning, with traces of blood left behind.
We immediately called emergency and explained to them the continuing symptoms. They told us to bring him in for another examination, so we did.
Blood results came back and it was seen that his kidneys were not in a healthy standing, as the clogged bladder added pressure to them, which needed to be relieved. His bladder remained full and tight, and the only option left was to have him hospitalized and looked after to ensure survival. 
Jasper is currently in great hands with the team at VEC (Veterinary Emergency Clinic), he is being given intravenous fluids and catheterization for the next few days to treat his Feline lower urinary tract disease (FLUTD), along with another procedure to ensure his kidney’s come back to a healthy standing and reduce the risk of future kidney damage.
It’s been an emotional and financially stressful time, as this came out of left field. Our home is simply not the same without him—he has so much more life to live, we needed to do the right thing.
The current vet fee’s are extremely high and sit at an estimated $6,222.00 CAD, which is not feasible for us to take on alone—especially not with the long-term dietary supplements and veterinary visits needed to keep him healthy and reduce the risk of future obstruction.
If you feel called to help Jasper, we truly do appreciate it from the bottom of our hearts.
Any little bit helps, even simply exchanging the value of your morning coffee.
If you are unable to donate, sharing this GoFundMe link is just as impactful and appreciated.
Thank you, thank you, thank you.
Celina & Matthew

On the evening of October 28, 2022, Diane Elaine (Schwartz) Evans was received at last into the arms of Jesus. Her 75 years on this Earth were gift to all who were privileged to know her. While she battled Alzheimer's bravely for the last 14 years, that will not be her legacy. Her legacy is love.
 As her children our greatest gift is the love story she shares with her husband David, her beloved for 53 years. They met in 1968 when they were both young, and working at the convalescent hospital in Lodi California. They married June 22nd 1969 with little money and no prospects but they had each other and that was all they needed.  Theirs is a love story for the ages. Despite the struggles and challenges that 53 years and 3 children can bring, they always remained devoted to each other, supporting one another through better and worse. Many remark on the incredible devotion that our father, Dave had for Diane as Alzheimer's slowly took her, but he would tell us that Mom gave him all her best years, how could he do any less for her now when she needed him most? She sewed our clothes, canned every food imaginable, she was an awesome cook, PTA president, room mom, and homework checker. She read us books, played games, and the memories of our family vacations keep us laughing until our sides ache. She went back to school to become a nurse while we were young and her example of sacrifice and dedication inspire us still. She was healer both at home and to all she came in contact with. When we each married she loved our spouses in equal measure. Always supportive and always wanting our happiness. 
But we believe the job she loved best of all was being a Nana. Known to her 4 beautiful grandchildren as "Nana Tickle", she was larger than life and always ready with love and hugs. She made songs for her grand babies, crocheted blankets, and would do anything for them. They were her brightest jewels in a very crowded crown. 
The love she had for her family seemed without bounds.  It began of course at first with her parents Jeanette Emhoff and John Henry Schwartz. Many older adults and injured civilians cannot handle the stress of a bus ride to get to areas of assistance. Ambulances can also travel after dark when other vehicles are not allowed to travel because of curfews. Ambulances also serve as a perfect hub to store useful pharmaceuticals.

This is Crystal Jones. Many people around Atlanta know her as grandmother. What follows is an opportunity for the community to rally around a woman that does so much for so many, and now needs our support in return.
Crystal is a modern-day Mary Poppins. She might show up to watch your kids for the night with a bounce house. On weekends, she drives around a 15-passenger van, picks up a gaggle of kids and takes them out on incredible day-long adventures. They return home tired, fed, and so happy. Their parents have had a full day to themselves. Crystal provides the most exceptional care for children all over metro Atlanta, and she will tell you it's because she raised 4 kids on her own and she wants parents to feel supported in ways she never did.
Her smile is infectious and her warmth can be felt at 200 yards. She manages to provide support for so many families, and she wants to start a business (the website is almost finished!). But when she goes home from caring for others' kids, she cares for two adult children with disabilities under the direst of circumstances.
Crystal is the most enterprising, entrepreneurial person you will ever meet, but she is underwater caring for her sons and dealing with a medical system and housing system that keep shutting them out. She has worked for decades to find solutions, to work the systems. But they're just not working for her. That's where we come in.
1. Steaven
Crystal's adult son Steaven was diagnosed with schizophrenia as a teenager. It has taken years to find the right combination of medicines that help him be comfortable and communicative (such as a monthly shot of Invega). But Georgia Medicare has declined to cover that medication. Without insurance, it's $1,200 a month. That's almost half of the family's income. Without the medication, Steaven's condition becomes severe and he suffers tremendously, sometimes wanders off. Recently, during a particularly bad episode, he was arrested. The danger of mental illness for young Black men is exponentially greater because police often see them as a threat. Steaven's medicine is critical for his life, his safety, and the peace and safety of his family.
One of the only ways Crystal can get support for Steaven is when his condition is severe enough that he can be committed to a county hospital. That triggers some emergency support that only lasts a few weeks after he is hospitalized. It's traumatic for Steaven and for Crystal.
2. Ronald
Meanwhile, Crystal is also caring for her other adult son, Ronald, who was paralyzed several years ago. Their home is not wheelchair accessible, and Crystal has to move her son in and out of the bathroom on a wheeled desk chair in order to fit through the door. While she has sufficient income and savings to afford a better apartment or even a down payment on a house, because she is self-employed she hasn't been able to get a loan or provide sufficient income verification to find an accessible three-bedroom rental. They have been taken advantage of by an unethical landlord who has refused to repair their hot water. The family has been living without running hot water for more than four months.
Crystal's dream is to live in a quiet place with lots of woods where she and her sons can enjoy the outdoors. She wants peace and calm for Steaven. She wants Ronald to be able to access the bathroom on his own (and he would like that, too!)
We are raising funds:
To underwrite Steaven's medication so he can get stable and he and Crystal can work on a plan together for his long term care
To pay enough advance rent that the family can move to an accessible apartment
We are also looking for an attorney who may be able to help with Steaven's case
If you can lend a hand navigating the Medicare system for mental health in Georgia (or you know another place in the Southeast where they can find better care), if you have connections to a pro-bono attorney or better housing for this family, please reach out.
Thank you!

When I asked him to prove that he was truly calling from the Sheriff's department, the phone number on my screen verified it as Scott County's Sheriff's department. I also Googled this number and confirmed it myself. I then was able to confirm that the name given to me was in fact the name of a Sergeant that worked for the county. This entire phone call I was being threatened with arrest and told I needed to resolve this matter immediately. At this point I was in the middle of a panic attack and incredibly concerned for my career, so I moved forward with the transaction to "pay my bond." I was then told to go to the Hennepin County's Sheriff's Department, where a detective informed me that I had been scammed and instructed to file a police report. I have since filed fraud claims, a police report, and contacted my bank. Due to the nature of how the funds were stolen, it is almost certain that we will not be able to track who did this or recover my money. I was told this type of scam is nearly impossible to trace.
I have also contacted local news stations, the MN Board of Behavioral Health & Therapy, the clinic I contract with, and I am notifying any person I know who works in the mental health field about this. It was a big life lesson for me, and it is now my goal to make sure this does not happen to anyone else.
The amount stolen from me was everything I had in my savings account. This money was set aside to cover things like rent, health insurance, student loans, and all of my other bills. It was also funds for the wedding of Nate, my fiance, and I in October of 2023 that I had regularly been setting money aside for. I no longer have a safety net, and the money I do have will be depleted quickly. I recently began working as a therapist in an independent contractor role, which has come with a very different pay schedule than I was accustomed to and is not necessarily consistent. As I am still building my caseload, I was heavily relying on my savings to carry me through this transition period -- and without it, I am in trouble.
I completely understand that in today’s economic environment everyone is struggling and trying to stay afloat. Asking for financial support is not something I take lightly or thought I would ever need to do. Any funds contributed will be used for paying bills, rent, living expenses and to make sure we are able to fulfill the contracts Nate and I have signed with wedding vendors. I'd also like to ask that you share this information with anyone you know who works in mental health/social work -- after researching online, this is a scam happening all over the nation, specifically targeting the innocent workers who are in these roles.
I sincerely appreciate everyone's love, support, kind words, and actions. I consider myself incredibly lucky to have the folks in my life that I do. I believe in the power of community, and promise to work diligently to find avenues to pay it forward once I am stable.
Thank you for taking the time to read this and for your consideration.

Some of you who receive this may already know some, parts, or all of the story. For those who do not let me introduce you to Stormageddon, The Dark Lord of All aka "Stormy". Don't let his grim-sounding name scare you or dissuade you from helping out. Storm is a 2 1/2 yr old fluffy and friendly St. Bernard. Stormy is the 2nd St. Bernard in the family, so they are no strangers to the issues that may befall a giant breed dog. 
Stormy is a purebred Saint they purchased from a breeder who made statements to the effect that:Quoting from their web (Facebook) FAQ
"· Are registered with AKC (American Kennel Club)"
"· Do not have history of hip dysplasia or any other genetic health issues"
"· Previous litters (from our Saint parents) do not have any history of hip dysplasia or any other genetic health issues"
There were a couple of testimonials and they thought nothing of the issue and reasonably relied upon the statement. They picked out one of the pups and put down a deposit, later paying quite a bit of money for him and taking him home to meet everyone.
Unfortunately, they took it on face value that those statements were true and now have found themselves with a vet bill of over $9000, excluding the costs I know they have already expensed up to this point. 
As a puppy, Stormy was like all puppies, very playful and excited to see people and have a good time rolling around and playing in the yard. They noticed early after his 1st birthday or so that he was not a big fan of going on walks, even just around the block. They thought nothing of it at the time and knew Saints were somewhat lazy, sometimes stubborn dogs. Towards the next birthday, they noticed he would limp a bit and not put pressure on his left leg, but it wasn't often, so they chalked it up to a minor issue. 
Eventually, it became more frequent, and they took him to the vet, who initially diagnosed a sprain, gave him some medication, and ordered less activity (not sure how you can get any less active, lol). The issue did not subside, so they had xrays ordered, and the complete picture of the problem was obvious. Stormy's left hip never developed, and his right hip socket was not fully formed either. They sent the xrays off to a specialist in Frederick (Skylos), who multiple vets and others highly recommended. He was examined thoroughly by Dr. Peter Lotsikas, and his staff at Sklos (https://www.skylossportsmedicine.com). Dr. Lotsikas reviewed the xrays and noted significant muscle atrophy because Stormy carries all his weight on his front two legs. He confirmed this is a genetic issue; unfortunately, the only options were a life of pain or a hip replacement. 
Skylos was founded in 2015 by Dr. Lotsikas and is the leader in their field. Skylos works up a flat fee guaranteed follow-up without additional costs. The total bill for Stormy would be a total of $9590.00. 
They, unfortunately, do not have a pile of money stashed in the walls of their house or a rich uncle to call. They have always been generous with others, sometimes to a fault, and hope that generosity will be revisited upon them. I know it is humbling and it pains them to ask for help from others. They, however, in this case, are asking on behalf of little (well, not so little) Stormy. Let Stormy know if you have some spare change, a dollar or two, or a rich uncle we can borrow for a bit. 
If we raise more than needed for the procedure by some miracle, we will donate any remaining funds to local animal charities such as For Otis Sake and The Washington County Humane Society, etc. Feel free to suggest others. Thank you for reading all of this. Please feel free to forward and share this story.

Hi, my name is Lisa McCarron. I’m Co-Founder & Director of Paddy’s Pasture, a nonprofit, 501c3 animal sanctuary in Central Virginia. 
This is a special fundraiser for a special cat.
I'd like to introduce you to Lettuce. 
Lettuce received his name after he showed up and made himself at home in a garden bed outside a house in North Florida.
His new humans had zero intention of acquiring a new pet, but Lettuce chose them and demanded they be his people. 
How does this make him special? Strays show up all the time, right? I’m glad you asked.
This year has been rough for Lettuce’s newly adopted humans. They have endured multiple losses of beloved people and pets in recent months, as well as the monetary and emotional costs associated with these events. 
And then along came Lettuce. It’s almost as if he showed up just at the right time, to offer some much needed smiles and extra love to them in their time of need- and that is something we want to make sure they continue to enjoy for many years to come.
Recently, Lettuce’s mom reached out to me asking for an opinion on a wound he had shown up with. I contacted a veterinary professional friend who was able to offer suggestions of wound care. His people have been diligently cleaning his boo-boo for him twice daily, every day, and it appears as though he is healing.
However, Lettuce needs a formal vet visit to ensure his present and future health. That’s where this fundraiser comes in.
I have contacted an animal hospital local to Lettuce’s home, and was able to get a quote for his initial care- they even gave rescue pricing for part of it. Visit/exam, FeLV/FIV testing, and rabies vax/tag will cost just a little over $100. From there, they will be able to determine if he needs any treatment for what appears to be a ruptured abscess.
Lettuce is already neutered, so given his demeanor, it is highly likely he was dumped or left behind by his previous people, as he was never claimed.
With neuter already taken care of, this means aside from general vet care and wound care, we would love to also raise enough to cover cost of microchip, preventatives, and a cat house for his time outdoors. Lettuce lives in a rural area, so much like our barn cats, he is living in an area that is considered safe for outside venturing. Veterinary care is the highest priority, but any additional funds raised will go to help supply Lettuce’s family with other feline necessities like food, etc.
When Lettuce first arrived, his new parents looked into rescues and no kill shelters and, as so many people nationwide are being told, they were all full. After briefly considering a local county shelter, they couldn’t bring themselves to leave him at one, knowing that intake overflow is resulting in shorter adoption windows and higher euth rates.

Can you help Lettuce continue to be a joy and comfort to his new family?

We would go back and forth between Hawaii and California for family trips, so luckily we were able to see and spend time with her at those times. The last time we saw her was this last June ‘22 and we didn’t think it would be our very last time together.
We were told the news almost exactly 1 week ago (Oct. 9th ) from today that she was pregnant and expecting pups…this would have been her Ist litter. It was sudden news that no one saw coming, no one knew she was even pregnant. She hasn’t had a period in about a year and she was approaching 7 years of age, so we already knew she was a high risk pregnancy. Once hearing this news over the phone, we were honestly quite angry because she had gone basically the entire pregnancy without any type of prenatal care or extra attention, because no one knew…
Luckily we had some family/close friends available to watch over her until we were able to fly over. At this time, Luna had been throwing up quite frequently; we were able to schedule an apt for her over the phone to be seen by her vet. In 2017/2018, Isaiah Shepard, began walking a path that seemed like "normal" teenage behavior. He started smoking pot and occasionally drinking with his buddies. They were still typical teenage boys. They loved skateboarding and were passionate about graffiti. As the years progressed different drugs were added to the mix. Isaiah and his friends got in trouble with the law a few times, but nothing too serious.
I recall the countless hours of heart-to-heart conversations we had. The tears, the promises, the weeks of being grounded, the hundreds of dollars spent on counseling...
It was a slow progression, and yet as I sit here typing it feels like it happened overnight. One day my once sweet baby boy, a loving brother, quick-witted, compassionate, respectful, and a responsible young man lost sight of who he was. It wasn't until the summer of 2020 that his problem was undeniable. He asked for help...
I began my search. Law enforcement, probation officers, judges, counselors, psychiatrists, out of state treatment facilities (all of which cost my years salary for a 30-day program). No one could help. He was my responsibility. My "problem" to fix. Countless sleepless nights. Hours of phone calls. One brick wall after another. It wasn't until Isaiah turned 18 that doors finally opened. Unfortunately, by this point, he was suffering from drug-induced psychosis. He had mentally checked out of reality.
What if I could have helped Isaiah sooner??
My son's story isn't unique. There are thousands of parents out there crying for help, help that just doesn't exist. This HAS to change. I refuse to allow Isaiah to be another number, another statistic. His death will not go in vain. Please help me bring awareness to the lack of mental and drug addiction services in Escambia County.
Over 4,700 people aged 15-24 years old died of an overdose of illicit drugs.
11.2% of all overdose deaths are between the ages of 15-24 years old.
More than 75,000 people have died from opioids in 2022 with Fentanyl being the leading cause.
Over 107,000 people died of drug overdoses in 2021, with over 8,000 of those deaths being in the state of Florida.
788,000 teenagers aged 12 to 17 years old met the criteria for drug use disorder within the last year.
The last letter I wrote to Isaiah...
I have bailed you out of jail.
I have given you a lawyer.
I have sent you to counseling and now treatment.
I have put myself in a financial crisis to save your life.
I will continue to repair the damage you have caused and mend the broken hearts.
I will love you until I take my final breath.
I know it is hard right now, but this is not where your story has to end.
As long as there is breath, there is still hope.
My son is gone. I can't bring him back. But I refuse to allow this to be where his story ends. Together as a community, we CAN make a difference.
Please join us on November 12th at the Graffiti Bridge to help bring awareness to the seriousness of Fentanyl and the lack of mental and drug outreach programs for adolescence in Escambia County.
Mural Painting will begin at 8:00am. The Sheriff and Chief of Police will be joining the cause at 11:00am. 
** Please wear green for mental health awareness and purple for overdose awareness. 
DONATE. 100% of all donations will go towards starting a program to help struggling families and teens in this county.
Thank you for your love and support.

This is my sweet boy, Squash Hammy Croissant.
Yesterday morning, while playing with his favorite toys, Squash stopped to lay down and started showing signs he wasn’t feeling good. An otherwise healthy kitty - up to date on his vaccines and check-ups, and a happy, active boy - his symptoms were worrisome and within a couple of minutes he was quickly declining. We headed to the vets for an emergency appointment, but when Squash was becoming unresponsive and struggling to breathe, we were transferred to a bigger emergency animal hospital nearby, where the doctor gave us the worst kind of news: Squash is battling heart failure.
Taken into immediate treatment - oxygen, IVs, and close monitoring - the doctor noted Squash’s temperature was rapidly decreasing and an examination revealed a masked heart disease, impacting his ability to breathe and leaving his lungs filled with fluid. The first priority was getting Squash’s body stabilized again, which the doctor compassionately warned may not be a possible outcome. In that case, we would have to say a very unexpected and oh too soon goodbye. We decided to continue the treatments for the recommended 24-48 hours and then go from there, all while keeping a close watch on Squash and making sure his healing and comfort were the main focus of every decision.
After spending the night at the hospital, Squash was seen by a cardiologist this morning to assess his condition. He has a type of heart disease that will need additional care, but once stabilized in the hospital for a few days of treatment, he has the hope of returning home to his favorite things, soaking in sun puddles, and being surrounded by his family. 
And as of this afternoon, Squash is already responding to treatment - his temperature is rising out of hypothermia, he is becoming more responsive, and he is slowly coming back to us. He is still on oxygen while the doctors are working to strengthen his breathing and get the remaining fluid out of his lungs, but we got the best gift we could ask for today: hope. With a detailed plan and attentiveness to it, Squash has the hope of not just coming home again, but feeling like himself and enjoying the rest of his days without suffering. 
Our life together only began earlier this year, and while I’m eternally grateful for each moment we have, I want to make sure Squash has a fighting chance to spend more time doing the things he loves and being around the people who love him.
Coming home will also require us to start a careful care routine - including daily medication and regular checkups. Unlike the case for many hospitals for humans, animal hospitals often require payment before treatment - and in the case of an emergency like this, it can be a really terrifying challenge to find the means to pay for treatment, knowing a little one’s life depends on it. Finding a way to afford the treatment when you can’t afford to lose any time. I can’t bear the thought that money would get in the way of Squash getting the care he needs.
Right now, the cost of his remaining hospital treatments, medication and outpatient care is estimated to be around $4,000. 
Asking for money is definitely out of my comfort zone, but for Squash, I want to give him every chance I can.
Thank you for hearing our story, sharing, or supporting in any way you can. It means the whole world.

On Saturday morning (10/22/2022), a guest at The Dog Park at Immanuel (Indianapolis, IN) pulled up to the park and saw eyes looking at her that didn’t quite belong - when she saw there was also a bowl of food, she realized that someone had dumped their dog at the park and that she was all alone.
The poor girl was skin and bones and couldn’t stand or walk on her own. Luckily this guest has a heart of gold and took her to IndyVet Emergency Services to get her help and notified a board member of the park.
We rushed to the vet right away to see if there was anything we could do for this poor pup - as you can see from the photos, she is extraordinarily emaciated/underweight. She also had fleas and needed to be tested for other illnesses. Indy also has refeeding syndrome, which happens when dogs are malnourished. She would have been sent to a shelter unless someone could pay for her expenses, and she would have likely been euthanized due to her condition and the shelters in Indianapolis being at capacity.
This is Indy at the vet. You can't see it in this picture, but they set up a little tablet for her to watch TV!
One of our fantastic board members immediately fell in love with those sweet eyes and agreed to give her a home - one where she will be loved and incredibly happy! They named her Indy Imm after the park, and she is improving daily. This campaign is to cover Indy’s vet expenses.

Well, it seems like most of us are destined to reach out for help from time to time, even for our pets. Sadly, this is our time. 
We were faced with an emergency with our Callie cat this week, and she is currently in the Pet Hospital up in Bellingham receiving care; we hope to bring her home tonight or tomorrow morning.
Callie has no prior health issues, and we take great care of her with regular checkups and vaccinations are current.    She’s still young at 7 years old. 
She became ill last Wednesday after being lethargic for 18 hours, not taking any food (which she always has access to dry food and begs for her wet food often) or using her potty box.    She ate a little of her dinner Wednesday night and nothing since, but she was drinking some water.    I took her to her regular Vet on Thursday and found a 104+ fever of unknown origin; they gave her an antibiotic shot and fluids and sent us home to monitor.    
We continued to monitor her food/water intake, which was very minimal water and checked her potty box every time she was up.    She slept a lot and continued to be lethargic and grumbling every time we tried to get her to take food and water.   We set up a camera to monitor when she came to her food and water with no results, and by Saturday night, we felt the situation was worse. If we had to wait until Monday to see her vet again, we would be looking at a Critical Situation.    All Vet hospitals in Western Washington are hard to get into and run at capacity, which is why we ended up in Bellingham, an hour away.     She was given more fluids, lab work, an anti-nausea medication, pain medication, and an appetite stimulant.  We had the option to admit her for ultrasound and further care, and we chose to try and see if the care they gave her would get things moving in the right direction, so we were allowed to bring her home.  After 24 hours, no food or water intake happened with a minimal urine output; it was time to get her back to the ER for admission for Ultrasound and further treatment, which included IV fluids, NG tube for nutrition, sedation for ultrasound and tissue samples.
We had some excellent news today concerning her eating.    She’s been offered baby food twice with good results and is now interested in eating.   The ultrasound shows Pancreatitis and general inflammation of the liver, spleen & intestines, which can be expected from not eating.    So far, it’s non-cancerous; we’ll have a better idea of what the future holds when the tissue results are in.    Hopefully, it will just be a diet monitoring plan.   Keeping my fingers crossed and praying a lot.   
Our costs by the time we are through getting her stable and home are looking to be about $5000.   This situation has been gut-wrenchingly stressful, and we don’t want to give up on our girl.     We’ve had to pay upfront through CareCredit, which is just about maxed out.     We are asking for help to cover some of these unexpected costs.     Any donation, no matter how great or small, would be greatly appreciated!    
Thank you so much for your consideration,    
Ronna & Stuart Blomgren

On Tuesday, November 8th there was a devastating house fire at Justin’s. His incredibly loved and spoiled two 9-month-old kittens were both in the house; Gus for at least 45 minutes, Frankie for at least 2 hours. Frankie, sadly, was only able to be taken out of the house after he collapsed.
A very caring EMT named Donna held both boys with oxygen masks in the back of the ambulance; Gus was foaming at the mouth and Frankie was wheezing, struggling to breathe. Once Justin and his girlfriend arrived, they were able to rush them to Floyd Harbor Animal Hospital, where the boys immediately received more oxygen and an initial assessment that required another urgent ride to East End Veterinary Center. The cost estimate for getting Gus and Frankie the care they needed to survive at East End was a minimum of $10,000; the boys were rushed regardless of the financial cost.
They were placed in oxygen cages once they arrived at East End and another assessment revealed Frankie was blind from the smoke, and possible carbon monoxide, inhalation trauma of the fire which deprived his brain of oxygen. The prognosis was guarded, but the boys began receiving the best care they could get: the oxygen cages, IVs of fluids, and nebulizer treatments of medication to help open their airways.
Gus (photos above); Frankie (photos below)
As of the evening of November 9th, we’re ecstatic to say that the boys continue to improve. Frankie still has a loss of vision but we are all hopeful that more oxygen and nebulizer treatments help him to regain some, or even all, of his vision. They are both breathing comfortably on their own - Gus out of the oxygen cage and Frankie still in the cage - and eating and drinking. Justin and his girlfriend were able to visit the boys in the afternoon and spent time holding them and letting the boys reconnect with eachother as well.
We’re very optimistic that the boys will make a full recovery, and we know Frankie will live a very full life with his brother Gus despite not having his complete vision. Justin adores these boys; they have remained his primary concern since the fire happened, and he is doing everything he possibly can to ensure they are the healthiest and happiest cats ever. Absolutely any donation will make a huge difference on the road to getting the boys home and paying off the vet care bill. We sincerely thank you in advance!
A HUGE thank you to all the amazing people who have contributed to the boys doing so well: the firefighters that pulled the boys from the house; Donna, for staying with them and giving them the love and oxygen they needed until Justin and his girlfriend arrived; and the wonderful people at Floyd Harbor Animal Hospital and East End Veterinary Center for responding so quickly and effectively to two traumatized kittens, and for being in constant communication to ease the anxiety of the situation. My name is Jordan and my girlfriend is Paige. I am writing this on behalf of our beloved rescue-dog, Turbo. I know many of you have dogs or pets that you couldn’t bear the thought of losing, especially when it’s not their time and they still have so much life left, so I am writing to you, asking for help.
      Turbo did not choose the hand he was dealt and a lot of people seeing his hand would fold, but we have not, and will not. When we first got turbo, almost three years ago now, he was a sickly sight. His ribs and hip bones protruded due to a lack of feeding, his muscles were atrophied due to a lack of exercise, his hair was missing from the shoulder blades down and covered in open sore’s and scabs due to a severe skin infection, and he was covered in scars due to God only knows what. He had been severely abused and neglected at the very least. We never met the previous owners, so we had no back story except for the way he looked, which couldn’t lie, unlike the people that did that to him would have. 
     When we first brought him home, he was good with people; skittish, but good. He would shy away from strangers at first, but once he warmed up, he was the biggest cuddle bug you’d ever meet! The only problem at the time is that he didn’t like the other animals, so we had to keep our other pets separated. We eventually hired a professional trainer, but she was fearful of him and worked indirectly, through us, only furthering the isolation.  
     A few months into being part of the family he began showing aggression towards people.  At this point, as responsible owners, we had to muzzle and leash him around strangers to protect them and him. His aggression—which is fear based, combined with believing he must protect my girlfriend and me from this world that he remembers as so cruel—has made it so he must be kept away from any human or animal except my girlfriend and me. 
     So, Turbo now lives in a large cage, only able to venture out when no one else is around and all other animals are secured.  And even then, we must worry about him somehow encountering another person or animal.
     We have healed his body from what people have done to him, but not his mind, thus far.  Short of the unthinkable, his veterinarian has suggested a particular rehabilitation center. The rehab is going to start around $7,000 and they will keep him in their facility for at least 3 months, to retrain his brain to be the loving good boy we know him to be; but not just with us, with everyone else too. Rehabilitation comes with no absolute guarantee, but he has a lot of love in him, and a lot of life, being only five years of age. 
     I won’t be the one to fold his cards, no matter what. 
     I Hope the picture and story will help you decide he is worth all the help he can get. Anything to help would be greatly appreciated. All Donations will go towards his rehabilitation, meds, and whatever else the world throws at him in this healing journey. Thank You, more than words.

He was the only man in history to win (6) NCAA College Titles in Wrestling, despite his high school not even having a wrestling team... 
A legend on the offensive line of some of the greatest Steeler teams in history & Pro Bowl selection who was drafted despite never playing high school or college football...
Carlton Haselrig was a man of incredible athletic ability and a drive to excel in everything he did. Still, even with great heart & spirit to accomplish these feats, he could not beat the monster that is Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy or CTE.  
Unable to work and bedridden, Carlton filed a claim in 2017 for the NFL Concussion Settlement, which was later denied due to the adjusted 'race norming '  on the cognitive scoring, despite having all the symptoms and testing to affirm a CTE prognosis. 
While Carlton had earned a pension from the NFL from playing in the league, his benefits were stopped the day he passed. In the documentary released on 11/16/2022, his battle with CTE in his final years is heart-wrenchingly shared in,  Bloodsport How the NFL failed its black players
In June of 2021, the #NFL agreed to stop race-based testing, which allowed Carlton's widow, Michelle, to refile his claim. During the arduous process, the loss of the pension and denial of the first claim devasted Michelle financially. She had $5 in her account at the time of the documentary production and was being forced to possibly sell Carlton's medals and keepsakes to make ends meet. She desperately needs your help now.
Through this GOFundME, the goal would be to provide Michelle and her family with a means to cover basic necessities and catch up on her house payment until she can find gainful employment or the second settlement can be processed & hopefully awarded. Without this fund or your caring support, Michelle will likely lose the family home and be unable to sustain herself long enough for a potential award to be made. 
I met Michelle after seeing her brave story in the Bloodsport documentary and felt compelled to act. I was connected via a mutual friend as part of my non-profit, 4CTE by CTE, which assists in locating resources & support for caregivers and warriors with suspected CTE. This fund is made with her approval and blessing, with 100% of all proceeds going directly to her for immediate emergency use. She has also graciously provided personal pictures used to share her family story.
The Steelers Fans are some of the greatest and most loyal people in the world of sports and undoubtedly will rise up to help one of their own. For the NFL enthusiast and humanity at large, this social injustice of profits over athletes should be our concern too. Please consider providing what you can and share this campaign to help the widow of a great man who left everything on the field, including, sadly, his life. Thank you and God Bless.
RIP #77 Carlton Haselrig

My name is Eddie, and I need your help. Today.
I am employed by, and live with, Tiffany and Tommy. My sole job is to keep rats and mice out of our home. Sad to say, I failed.
About three months ago two rats, nicknamed Bonnie and Clyde, somehow entered our home and set up their abode in our stove. Bonnie and Clyde are no ordinary rats; they are super intelligent, clever, cunning & evil. In the course of their stay here they have damaged our couch, countless items of clothing, the stove, dishwasher, a brand-new high-end backpacking gear, ruined piles and piles of food, and disrupted our sleep with their brazen, callous, noisy eating habits. They were actually taunting us by advertising where they were, knowing we could not catch them.
I say “we could not catch them,” but it was actually my full-time job to do so. Tiffany and Tommy lent a hand by deploying every rat trap known to man, to no avail. It was a true head-scratcher: How is it possible for two rats to escape capture within the confined space of a home?
Well, two days ago the tide finally turned. With every food item out of reach, they resorted to foraging in the hall closet, where the aforementioned backpack (with some protein bars) was stored. Did I mention there is one door in/out of the closet, and that this is a very confined space? When I awoke, I picked up the scent immediately, (yes, I smelled a rat) but also detected their physical presence. So I tiptoed in, which is hard for a dachshund to do, identified the first enemy, and attacked.

Megan Michelle Holloway unexpectedly passed away Tuesday, November 8, after losing consciousness and going into cardiac arrest. She was only 24.
 
Megan, a lifelong animal lover, worked at the Bank of Oklahoma as a vault specialist but always dreamed of working with animals. Her only fear was if she could deal with the pain of losing them if they were ill or dying.
 
Her family never knew what animal she would bring home. 
 
“She fed a family of raccoons. All of them would let her pet them,” her father Jeff Holloway said. “When someone told me about a baby rabbit that obviously had lost its momma, I told Megan about it and a couple hours later she was back at the house with the rabbit. Fed it from a dropper and then bottle until it was big enough to let go.
 
“She’s had guinea pigs, a gecko, a skunk, cats and, of course, two of her best friends — Zoey, a rat terrier, and Mia, part corgi/miniature pinscher.”
 
She graduated from Sand Springs' Charles Page High School in 2016, overcoming many odds.
 
Megan suffered a traumatic brain injury at 15 years old in an ATV accident and fought hard to regain her speech and mobility.
 
At the time, friends rallied around her, making T-shirts that read, “Team Megan” and “#prayformeganholloway.”
She had a tough medical life after that with various health issues, according to her mom, Renee Holloway. “She was such a fighter. She overcame most of it with a smile on her face. Many times she was suffering in silence. Her body was in physical pain most of the time. “
Family and friends are remembering Megan for that tenacity and toughness, but also for her sweet playfulness — her love of Scooby-Doo and a blanket that she’s had since birth that she’s never without. 
Megan was never empty handed when going to visit her family either. From toys for her nieces, nephew and younger brother and sister, which they usually had to find via a scavenger hunt, to bringing her big brother and sister whichever crumbl cookie she knew they would enjoy, Megan always thought of others first. 
 
People in the community may know Megan from her work at BOK and at various restaurants and the now-closed Ann's Bakery.
 
She leaves behind her father and mother, Jeff and Renee Holloway; siblings Ryan Holloway and his girlfriend Brooke Bellendir; Malorie Daugherty and her family, husband Randy, daughters McKenzie and Lakelyn and son Dawson; Evin and Emma Holloway; grandparents Mike and Marilyn Elliott; fiance Jordan Simpson, and many aunts, uncles and cousins.
 
Private graveside services have been set, but Megan’s family will receive visitors during a viewing at Dillon Funeral Service in Sand Springs from 6 to 8 p.m. Monday, November 14. A celebration of life is being planned for Saturday, November 19.
Her medical and funeral costs are mounting, and the family so appreciates everyone’s support. Thank you.

It is with a heavy heart to inform you of the passing of our one-of-kind amazing, beloved matriarch Sokhan Y on November 7 surrounded by her family.
Our mother, Sokhan Y endured challenges in her lifetime that most people would have given up- but not her. She was a warrior in every sense of the word. The second youngest of 13 children, Sokhan grew up working as a farmer in countryside northern Cambodia before becoming a hairstylist at 15 until her marriage at 18 to Chanthan Y, a school principal in 1968. She was also a seamstress, cook, and nanny.
In 1975, the communist Cambodia regime forced my parent apart- my father to be a soldier in the war, leaving my mother alone to raise their 5 young children. Sokhan, along with her elderly mother and five young children forced to leave their home to endure four years of unimaginable hardships and atrocities in the Khmer Rouge genocide camps. With mom’s tenacity and determination, our entire family beat the odds and survived when most did not. In 1979, after the war was over, she was reunited with my father in a refugee camp in Thailand. Their undying love truly beats all odds.
In 1981, our family emigrated to the United States under the sponsorship of First Methodist Church in Paris, TX and my parents worked as janitors in the local hospital. After 3 years they moved to California and became part of a flourishing Cambodian immigrant community in Stockton, CA. Mom was a migrant farm worker in the (with the whole family). She also turned our little apartment into a barber shop for the next 30 years- literally making her community beautiful. Countless smiles left her haircut chair feeling and looking better than when they came in because of her. On the weekends, mom and dad can be seen at the temple they helped create- helping and leading the community with ceremonies, weddings and funeral rituals. Any time she can, she would help- anyone. Sokhan Y is fiercely relentless and selfless, with the biggest heart. Her lasting legacy will live on in our family and her community family she built.
She is survived by her 6 children, 13 grandchildren and 8 great grandchildren. She is preceded in death by her husband of 55 years Chanthan (passed away two years ago this month), her late mother Mik Nuon and late father Chun Prom.
We are forever thankful and blessed to call her our mother (Mai), grandmother (yai), and great grandmother (yai thuot).

ABOUT MALCOLM
Malcolm was born on February 15, 1999, in Arlington, VA. From the beginning, Malcolm was intellectually curious and a happy baby. That curiosity, combined with his compassion and spirituality, exemplified what a truly unique and special person he was.
Malcolm had a love for learning and more profound knowledge. He attended Bible Study fellowship since he was two years old. In middle school, Malcolm was engrossed in robotics. He participated in numerous state competitions with his robotics team and even received awards for best programming.
His thirst for learning continued throughout his lifetime. He participated in summer learning activities across the country each summer in high school. During the summer of his sophomore year, he studied Chinese at Harvard University Summer School and Java programming at MIT through ID tech. Malcolm was selected to be on the National Foreign Language Honor Society for Chinese. Malcolm also published a science-fiction book for teens and played percussion during a European band tour with his high school band.
Malcolm's bilingual abilities helped fuel his love of travel. By the age of seventeen, Malcolm had visited over twenty-one countries, including a cultural exchange program in Cuba, when he was sixteen. Malcolm's love of people led him to participate in a mission trip that carried the word of God & school supplies to students in Jamaica.
After graduating from Kinkaid High School, Malcolm continued his pursuit of learning by attending New York University (NYU). He had an avid love of Marvel Comics and video games. Malcolm graduated with a Bachelor of Computer Science from NYU on May 19, 2022. He was well-loved by the student residents from the Goddard dorm at NYU and was awarded Student of the Month.
Malcolm was baptized by Pastor Eric Lacy and was a past member of True Love Church Youth Ministry. At the time of his passing, he was a member of The Woodlands Church Atascocita. Malcolm was also an active member of Jack and Jill of America.
Malcolm is survived by his loving parents, Raymond and Holly, along with his sister, Tiffany (Tyrone) Little-Saunders. His memory lives on with many aunts, uncles, cousins, extended family, and dear friends.

George Ybarra Lopez

Many of you have asked how Into the Light Horse Rescue and Sanctuary, a 501c3 non profit was started.
Since I am using my birthday to inspire my friends and my larger network to donate to my life’s passion, I would love to share our story here. 
It all began with Dove, a newborn foal. In 2015, on a Colorado feedlot that sold horses to slaughter, a young black and white mare with dreadlocks in her mane and tail, gave birth to this sweet filly with a little white dove marking on her side. The filly was born amongst the chaos of the feedlot, surrounded by 100 horses all awaiting their fate to be shipped to slaughter.
I had learned of the newborn foal and her Mother, and knew immediately they needed to be saved. Without hesitating, I paid for their freedom and had them rushed to a quarantine facility.
While Phantom and baby Dove were in quarantine, Dove developed an infection. Feedlots are no place for any horse -- especially a newborn. The disease and sickness Dove developed from being there for the first few hours of her life, compromised her ability to fight off infection. As infection attacked Dove’s eyes, she went blind before the vets had an opportunity to save her sight. Her illness continued to develop, and at exactly six weeks old, she succumbed to her sickness and passed away while her Mamma Phantom stood helpless.
The loss of baby Dove left me devastated. More than ever, I felt that she and the three other horses I had saved, needed to continue on for Dove. In the weeks following Dove’s passing, I saw the urgent need to stand up for the thousands of horses that continue to be tossed away and lost to the slaughter pipeline. So that Dove's loss would not be in vain.
Into the Light was born from this chain of events, and the name represents the feeling our horses experience when they are at the end of the line in the slaughter pipeline, but are brought back into the love and light of freedom when rescued.
Dove continues to inspire our rescue every day, and we carry on her memory with each horse we have the honor of saving. To date, we have rescued 90 horses, and intend to continue our mission of working tirelessly to ensure our horses are loved and cared for, and that they never again experience the horrors of the slaughter pipeline.  Our focus in recent years has been caring for our sanctuary horses, 
If you decide to donate, your valuable funds will be used to support our 10 special needs sanctuary horses.  Instead of buying your daily latte, could you spare $5 to help us buy the meds our sweet rescues need on a daily basis?
Thank you so much for reading this and for sharing on social media, by private messenger or text.

Hi there, my name is Rachel and this is my beloved crazy boy, Raisin. He's the type of cat that runs sideways down hallways. He enjoys digging in the bathtub and sink. He loves blue balls, and only blue balls. He loves boxes. So much so that when he's in one, we push him around the house and he sits there looking around. We call it his spaceship. He really is a character.
Raisin had a really rough life in the beginning. Found with both eyes glued shut with infection, underweight, half the size of his siblings. With a lot of love from the beautiful people that work at a cat shelter, he was nursed back to life. He's been living with me for the past two years and has made a huge impact on so many people. I think most of us can relate that animals make a special imprint on our lives. They are family. He's my kid.
Recently, we heard Raisin yowling in pain one morning. It looked like he was trying to pee but just couldn't make it happen. We rushed him to the emergency vet as regular vets were not open yet. He was taken to the back and we were later pulled into the exam room. After some blood work and a urinalysis he was then diagnosed with FLUTD (feline lower urinary tract disease) with urinary obstruction. What this means is that there were crystals in his ureter which were large enough to completely block the flow of urine. It's a very painful experience and if not treated, he could go into kidney failure.
Of course we wanted our boy to be healthy again so we allowed them to hold our kid for the next few days. In order for that to happen, we needed to fork out half of the estimated bill, over a thousand dollars. We had to take out a loan for that.
We picked Raisin up two days later (we had to take out two more loans to cover the rest of the bill, one in which I could lose my car). Raisin was pretty groggy which I expected, and they gave me meds for the next few days. He did well, slowly getting back to his routine.
And then, just a few days after I got him back, he started having a lot of blood in his urine. Not a good sign. He could get blocked again and then the whole process will start again...if we can pay.
So I am asking for help so I can get the right care for baby. I am disabled and he keeps me sane, he keeps me present and he reminds me that there is fun and good in the world. I can't do this without him. I need him to be ok.
So I am asking for help, both to help cover past bills and loans, as well as upcoming costs. Raisin deserves a chance to live a happy, healthy life. He's only two. He's got so much more living to do. Thank you so much for your donation. We are so so grateful to you.

Aaron Christopher Krask, 27, unexpectedly passed away on Thursday, October 20th, 2022.
Aaron was born April 29th, 1995 in Atlanta, Georgia to parents Elizabeth Lang Krask and Scott Robert Krask. Two years later, the Krask family grew and Aaron gained a sister, Lindsey Michelle Krask.
Aaron was an avid lover of the outdoors, a dedicated member of the school marching band, and always loved to tell jokes and play games with his little sister. Aaron began learning German in high school and applied for the CIEE exchange program, a decision that changed the rest of his life. Aaron was extremely passionate about all things German: language, culture, and exchange programs.
In the fall of 2014, Aaron began studying International Affairs and Germanic and Slavic Languages at the University of Georgia. While there, he met his wife, Allison Bernice Hardman, and eventually went on to graduate with a dual Bachelors degree in May of 2017. After that, Aaron began his Masters in German at the University of Georgia and began teaching for the German department. There, Aaron was able to inspire many others and share his passions.
Upon Aaron’s graduation from his Masters program in May of 2020, he went on to work at Bark Technologies as a Customer Support Specialist. There, Aaron was able to use his love of helping and talking to others to excel in his career. He made an abundance of friends at Bark. Eventually, in December of 2020, Aaron married Allison Hardman and the two of them bought a house together in Athens.
Aaron is survived by his wife, Allison Hardman, his parents, Beth and Scott Krask, his sister, Lindsey Duarte, his brother-in-law, Roberto Duarte, his paternal grandfather, Kenneth Krask, and his beloved four-legged children, Bella, Luke, Jaxx, and Jules. Aaron is survived by so many others including his German host parents, Helga and Heiner Kösters, and the remainder of his German family. Especially being so young, Aaron is also survived by a plethora of other family members and an incredible amount of friends.
He is preceded in death by his maternal grandparents, Barbara and Dale Lang, and his paternal grandmother, Joan Johnson Krask.
Aaron was so many things; a husband, a pet dad, a son, a brother, a friend, and a damn good Dawg.
In lieu of flowers, we ask for donations to a few of the many things that Aaron was so passionate about: CIEE (an exchange program that Aaron was a part of for 10 years), the University of Georgia’s German Department (where Aaron both studied and taught), and Middleton Memorial (a family memorial in his “own little slice of Heaven” Ludowici, GA).

Arthur “Arty” William Seabury, III of Wilmington, NC, aged 61, passed away suddenly at home on November 11, 2022.  He was born on October 26, 1961, in Renton, WA (while his Father was in Vietnam) and raised in Jacksonville, NC.  Arty was predeceased by his parents, Bernice Finch Seabury and Arthur William Seabury, Jr.  He is survived by his wife of 27 years, Susan, son Arthur “Will” William Seabury IV, granddaughter Juniper and dog, Schatzi; his step-mother Joan Barnes Seabury, sister Sherry S. Cook (Charley), brothers Bob (Kathy) and Ken (Mary) Finch; sister-in-law Cheran Harris (Farrell); nieces and nephews; step-siblings, other family and good friends too numerous to name.  
     In Jacksonville, Arty grew up the son of a Marine and an awesome Mom. He enjoyed camping trips, soccer, surfing, being with his brothers, and tormenting his sister.  He went to Infant of Prague, then graduated from Jacksonville Senior High in 1979.  He went on to UNC-Wilmington before enlisting in the US Coast Guard in 1981.  
     He served 4 years with the USCG, stationed initially at Governors Island, NYC, as well as other east coast posts, serving on the USCG Cutters Escape and  Cape Fairweather.  Arty, aka “Sting,” rose to the rank of QuarterMaster 3rd class, earning ribbons in 45 caliber and M16 marksmanship, as well as a Good Conduct Medal.  He loved his time and travels in the Coast Guard and made dozens of friends along the way.
     Arty returned to Wilmington in 1985 and, for over 35 years, was a Jack of all Trades - carpentry, electrical work, hurricane shutters, project supervision, facility manager, etc.  He found a way to fix anything he put his mind to.  Known to family and friends as a self-proclaimed “genius,” he was a constant source of advice and answers. With Muni as his home course, he was an avid golfer, enjoying years of rounds with some of his same friends each week.  He loved being on the water; was a soccer fanatic; huge St. Louis Cardinals baseball fan and UNC basketball fan; Blues lover, especially Eric Clapton; his favorite restaurant was Szechuan 132.  Arty was a proud husband, father, grandfather and friend to anyone he met.  He was a good-natured, kind man with a big smile who will be profoundly missed by all who knew him.  
     A Celebration of Life will be held in the weeks to come, with details to follow.  In lieu of flowers, please consider donating to a charity of your choice or The Arty Seabury Memorial Fund to help raise funds for funeral expenses and to establish a trust fund for his granddaughter, Juniper.
