Ilona Rymska, her mother Tanya, and 16-year-old daughter, Katrina, were living an everyday life in Marhanets, Ukraine, when Russia bombed their country. They had read about the Russian buildup on the border but couldn’t believe that Russia, which they considered a sister country, would actually attack. Hoping beyond hope that the invasion would end, they remained in their home until May 2022, when it became apparent that they had to flee for safety as the Russian army drew closer.
Leaving their home, lives, and all possessions with one suitcase and a violin, the three boarded a train traveling across western Ukraine to Poland, terrified as missiles flew overhead and exploded nearby.
From May to September, Ilona, Tanya and Katrina sheltered in a communal room in a damp, rundown hostel in Krakow, Poland. Two weeks ago, Ilona and her daughter were able to travel to the USA. As a non-citizen, Ilona’s mother has had to stay in the Krakow hostel, alone.
I met Ilona 20 years ago when she was living in the US, married to an American. During the ten years she was here, she earned her US citizenship, attended college and gave birth to a daughter. Divorced when her daughter was six years old, Ilona took her back to Ukraine where they started over, living a modern, fulfilling life with Tanya. That is, until Russia destroyed their home and lives.
Sixteen-year-old Katrina is a talented musician who speaks English, Ukrainian, Russian, French, and a bit of Polish. She has enrolled in the local high school and begun to make friends. Katrina hopes to join the high school’s honor symphony and Hendersonville’s local Youth Symphony during their upcoming auditions, and I think she will easily qualify. She’s a fantastic violinist!
Can You Be A Sponsor
In addition to financial donations, we seek a family, church, individual, or group to sponsor Ilona’s mother, Tanya, into the United States. United for Ukraine (U4U) is a government program specifically designed to bring Ukrainians who are displaced by war with Russia to the US. Under the terms of this program, Tanya would join Ilona and Katrina in the US and stay for up to two years. Please have a look at the program’s website: www.uscis.gov/ukraine.  Contact Dianne if you can sponsor.
Donations
Donations raised here will help Ilona pay for her car so she can work, accumulate the money she needs to qualify to rent an apartment, pre-pay a few months’ rent, and bring her mother to safety.
I can’t imagine the trauma of leaving my life forever with nothing but one suitcase and a violin.
Please help.

One of my elderly customers could always be seen with his trusty sidekick riding alongside him on his golf-cart (his only mode of transportation) to the mailbox at the end of his rural street.  One day in the late Spring, I saw him there, on the cart, without Lucy.  “Where’s your copilot?” I asked.  With big tears in his eyes, he told me he’d buried her earlier that morning.  He was heartbroken.  He postponed getting another dog for a few months, until I showed him the picture of “Oreo” at 13 weeks old.  She was one of a litter of 11 for whom another customer of mine was trying to find homes.  He was sold.  I picked up the sweet pup and took her to him.  As my customer has very limited means, I told him I’d take care of her immunizations.  I contacted a mobile vet in the county and explained the situation that I would be handling the financial part if they could just provide the care. 
 
It didn’t happen in time.  On October 15, I had a delivery in the neighborhood and stopped by to see the pup and my customer. Oreo had stopped eating the day before and had begun throwing up even her water.  I told him I’d check again the following day. 
 
That following day, she was terribly ill.  I called my boss and asked to get a driver in to take over my route so that I could get this pup to the vet, ASAP.  It was on a Sunday, so an Emergency Vet visit was the only option.  We booked it to the University of Florida School of Veterinary Medicine Small Animal Hospital where this poor little lady was diagnosed with parvovirus, a potentially fatal disease that can only be treated with supportive care of intravenous fluids, nasogastric feedings, medicine for pain, nausea, and appetite stimulants. 
 
Her health and recovery are of the utmost importance.  I’m doing everything in my power to provide for her care.  The initial visit/assessment/treatment was $346.  For the hospital admission, I agreed to a low-end estimate of $2500 and a high-end of $3500 and put down a deposit of $2700+.  These costs will rise even higher if her treatment lags on for more days than expected. 
I’m asking for your help, especially those of you who are pet lovers.  I can’t do this alone.  I feel obligated to help this man save his beloved pup and I’m obligated to her as well. 
 
Please find it in your hearts to help me help Oreo survive this dreadful disease by helping me cover the costs of whatever treatment is necessary. 
 
From the bottom of my heart, I thank you!

Hi everyone! A big update on Rue!He was misdiagnosed with Cataracts. His symptoms started with loss of vision. We took him to the ER, they referred us to an eye specialist and they diagnosed him with cataracts. Then soon after that he started developing other issues, such has his inability to move his back legs properly. He’s constantly falling over and has a really hard time getting around and using the potty. I took him back to the vet, they referred us to a neurologist, where he was then diagnosed with FIP. There are different forms of FIP, wet and dry form and then there’s ocular/neuro form, which is what Rue has. FIP is a viral disease that is caused by feline coronavirus. Its estimated that 80-90% of cats get coronavirus, but only 5-10% of cats get infected with FIP, and it is usually cats under 2 years old. Rue is only 5 months old. When I first got him, he could see and run and jump perfectly fine, this disease has slowly been making him deteriorate and it’s absolutely breaking my heart. He deserves to have a normal, fun and playful life that a kitten should have! Since FIP is such a new disease, when first started, there was no medication and no cure and it was a death sentence for kitties. Most would’ve survive over a couple months. Now that some time has gone by, there IS medication for it now, but because it’s so new, it’s not yet FDA approved. Which means I cannot get it through the vet. There are other ways to get this medication, and I’ve met some amazing people who are helping with that. The medication is supposed to reverse his symptoms and get him back to living a normal, healthy life! There is no “cure” for FIP, it will live in his body forever, BUT this medication will literally save his life. Without it, he will keep getting worse and he will die. I just started him on the medication but I only have a couple days worth, and will need to keep ordering more (84 days worth.) So, I would first like to say THANK YOU to everyone who has donated and everyone that plans on donating. I understand we don’t all have money to spare, so even a simple share will help us out! Please send lots of hope and prayers to our baby boy, Rue!! Let’s get him fixed up and feeling better! He’s such a strong boy that keeps fighting, I know we can do this! On September 28th F Building at Port Charlotte High School, which is where our band room and all of our equipment is located, was hit hard by Hurricane Ian and sustained a significant amount of damage.  As of now, the extent of the damage to our instruments, flags, and uniforms is not known as it will take some time to obtain an inventory and assessment for the cost to repair and/or replace what is needed.  
The PRIDE of Port Charlotte band program has been an extremely successful competitive band in Port Charlotte, Florida, for almost 40 years.  We use PRIDE as an acronym to summarize our standards we established for ourselves.  The acronym stands for Prepared, Responsible, Integrity, Discipline, and Energy.  The trophies that used to line the interior walls of the band room are now occupying over 60 boxes in storage pods.  Before the storm, the Marching Band, made up of over 80 students, had been practicing multiple days per week since before school even started in August to learn their 2022 competitive show to be judged at Districts on October 29th.  Due to the storm and the resulting inability to locate and repair/replace what we need coupled with the short time left to practice, the band is not going to be able to compete this season.  The decision was not made lightly but it is the realization we had to accept.  
Our goal now is to re-establish and rebuild this program.  The band room is home to the kids involved and to those who are alumni of the band.  The trophies are reminders of the success this program has had and the PRIDE that accompanies having participated in the program.  The uniforms we wear signify that we are a family and the music that our students play links us together as one.
We don’t know what our financial needs are going to be when everything is accounted for and things are settled but we do know that insurance will not cover everything and we are asking for help.  The goal for our request is set at one dollar because we do not want to ask for more than we need and we just cannot put a number to that at this point in time.  
“Music produces a kind of pleasure which human nature cannot do without” – Confucius 
Thank you in advance for your consideration to assist us, 
Corey Hoeben, Director of Bands and the Board of Directors, Port Charlotte High School Band Boosters

Su’Myrah Jones was born on November 9th, 2022. This beautiful baby’s entrance into this world wasn’t easy: she suffered a traumatic brain injury from a difficult birth.
Su’Myrah is only days old, yet we know that the life ahead of her and her parents will be a test of perseverance and faith.
Su’Myrah had severe brain damage. She has been diagnosed with HEI-Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. Her brain was deprived of oxygen for an undetermined amount of time, causing the death and decay of brain cells.
After her initial birth, she was transported to Cincinnati Children’s Hospital, where she underwent therapeutic hypothermic treatment to slow down the decay of her brain.
On November 14th, Su’Myrah and her parents received her MRI results: a vast majority of her brain has severe damage, including her brain stem.
Su’Myrah may never be able to walk. To talk. To sit on her own, or even swallow food. It’s difficult for doctors to give a solid prognosis for the rest of her life as right now, her life is being measured in minutes.
Her mother, Makayla and her father Del are keeping their faith in God. They are praying for a miracle. They love their baby girl and will do anything to make sure she has the best life possible, however long that life may be.
Once Makayla and Del can safely bring Su’Myrah home-after she is stable and after they are trained to take care of her medically, they will be moving in with Makayla’s family. 
But they need our help, too. Since this was not something that this family could ever have been prepared for, they need help to get the home ready for Su’Myrah. Del and Makayla don’t have a bed or clothing storage or a rocking chair. They were blessed with some items for their baby girl from their baby shower, however given the circumstances, their income has been greatly reduced in order for them to stay by their child’s side.
If you can, please help us. Help us support this young family with basic needs and future needs as well. Food and clothing and diapers and wipes. To pay their bills. Help us support them so that they can focus on their beautifully fragile little girl and bring her into a safe and happy and healthy home in which they can continue to ensure she has the fullest life she could possibly have.

My parents purchased Lexi and her sister, Sissy, from a breeder recently. They were told that they are both Maltipoos and are the cutest little pups ever! My parents are amazing people who believe that when you take a pet into your home, it is your responsibility to take care of them and ensure they have the best life, even if the cost is high.

After having them for five days, Lexi started showing signs of not feeling well but thought maybe she was stressed from the change. This quickly worsened, and they rushed her to an ER vet early on day seven. Once tested, they found out that she was positive for Parvo. Given that she is the runt of the litter and the suspicion that the breeder may have been using vaccines from a farm supplier instead of taking them to a vet, where the vaccines are kept in the right environment to ensure the highest potency, she had a huge mountain to climb to win this battle. They also tested her sister; she was negative for now and is being monitored continuously on a rice and chicken diet.
Lexi has been at the VCA Cottonwood Animal Hospital ER since that day but is fighting with everything she has. The vet has her on IV medications and are syringe feeding her multiple times a day. Until her diarrhea, white blood cells, and glucose return to normal, we cannot bring her home. Unfortunately, this means that each day the cost is increasing.
If you can help my parents cover the cost of Lexi's medical emergency, we would truly feel blessed by your generosity. Lexi will get the care she needs regardless, but the burden on my parents would significantly decrease.

My name is Justin Novak, the stepson of an amazing man, James Lapp. I was home on Leave in Ohio from the Air Force, currently stationed in Anchorage, Alaska. They loaded him into the ambulance and raced to the hospital, unable to establish a pulse before leaving the house. After returning home, my mom looked at us and said, "I know this may not be the right time, but I think I'm going to have to sell the house". My mom has given more of herself to take care of others than she has ever asked for. I had to convince her that maybe this time, she was the one who needed help. We are trying to raise enough money to help her pay for the funeral. We appreciate you taking the time to read this and can't express how thankful we are for any donations. We have received an overwhelming amount of support in just the first few hours, we never imagined so many people would bless us with open hearts. We are still working on the details for the funeral arrangements, but all of the estimates we have received are significantly more than our original goal. I hope you understand our decision to increase the goal and allow us to give Jim the funeral he deserves.

I feel like a failure for doing this, but I need some help supporting my family, and I don't know where else to go. Some people may frown upon me doing this, but I struggle to keep things together. I have been applying for jobs over the last six months with some luck, but not enough to pay our bills. I would instead like to be working a full-time job than have to ask for help. Please listen to my story, and if you can help me find a job or give my family a small donation to pay our mortgage and bills, it would be greatly appreciated.
Two and a half years ago, I was diagnosed with IBS, major depression, anxiety and PTSD from childhood traumas. I was working in a toxic work environment and started to suffer from panic attacks. I, unfortunately, had to leave my job after 22 years with the company. I was good at my job. At the time, I was going through therapy but didn't realize how long of a road this would be. I was prescribed medications that didn't work, attempted suicide three times, and was hospitalized twice. I felt like a complete failure and a burden to everyone.
I was finally diagnosed with celiac disease, which helped me understand why my IBS was so bad, but I also realized that my depression and anxiety exacerbated my physical symptoms. I have gone through many different medications and have continued to seek therapy. I could only support my family by using my 401k, which is now gone. I also tried to run a small business from home while I worked on my health. It kept me active and focused but did not provide enough money to support my family.
Everyone has difficult times; unfortunately, many suffer from traumas that we don't even know about. The best thing to do is seek help and be conscious of others' behaviors. They may be too scared or too proud to ask for help. They may feel like a burden and seclude themselves, living in a hole of dispare. That can be very destructive to their mental health. I know; I have tried my best to stay out of that hole.
I have had such a hard time finding a job. If there is anyone I can forward my resume to or anyone that can donate a small amount to help my family, I would be very thankful.
I love you all!
Christopher Barszcz

In addition to that, she was a committed member of the Scouting community and volunteered countless hours with them throughout the years.

The Make(HER) Collective, a Hampton Roads-based community of local women makers and business owners, is raising money to establish The Kandace Florence Memorial Scholarship and assist Kandace's family with the burden of memorial expenses.
Kandace departed this earth far too early on October 30th, 2022.
She traveled with two friends, Jordan Marshall and Cortez Hall, to Mexico City for the celebration of Dia de los Muertos. The three friends were found unresponsive in their Airbnb. The cause of death is still unknown.
We lost a massive light in our community when we lost Kandace, owner of Glo Through It candles + self-care.
She was by our side since the beginning- her unforgettable smile lighting the rows of every one of our women-owned Make(HER) Markets and many other special events.
In the small business world, many of us work at home alone. Kandace was our co-worker. 
She graced us through workshops with her expansive business & marketing knowledge and sought to reach and teach more women through our upcoming winter retreats.
She inspired us constantly with her honesty, her confidence, her vulnerability, and her unshakable motivation to grow her business.
We can't imagine our community without her, and we know the world had big things in store for her.... But not because she was given it- because she worked tirelessly for it. While still prioritizing self-love, rest, fun, and family.
In Kandace's honor, we are doing our best to Glo Through this impossibly difficult time, and we vow to carry on her legacy of self-care.
Our hearts are with her family during this time, and our goal is to raise at least $10,000 to support them in paying for memorial expenses.
The first $500 raised will establish the Kandace Florence Memorial Scholarship, which will provide one yearly, all-expenses-paid Make(HER) Collective Membership + Make(HER) Market registration & mentoring for a local maker.

Hello, fellow animal lovers! I've created this fundraiser to help my wonderful neighbors Emilie Christian and Max Lester's animal rescue, which recently suffered severe damage in a powerful storm on November 8th, 2022.

Goat barn was totaled
PVC water lines ripped from the ground and destroyed (side note, this community relies on well water systems, so water conservation is critical to all of us. 
Water troughs tossed in the air, cracked and destroyed
Trees uprooted and toppled over onto structures, including animal enclosures
Poultry fence and insulators crushed
Feed shed and protective tarps, and other necessary items destroyed

 Goals are as follows:
Complete rebuild of goat barn
Reinforcing chicken coops for safety, including sides and roofs 
Improve wind protection for all aviaries and large animal shelters 
Replacing all damaged items such as waterlines, fencing, feed storage, water troughs and even animal bedding.
These repairs and rebuilds will involve great material and labor costs such as lumber, large tool rentals, concrete, haul away / dump fees, and, needless to say, manpower. Any donation, large or small, is deeply appreciated.

Hello, for starters, my name is LeAndra Trefethen. Over the last six months, I have frequented a local neighborhood pond, and it’s no secret to those close to me that I’ve formed a bond with each and every one of the ducks that call this place their home.
 Unfortunately, 10 of these ducks are full-bred domestics that have been dumped, left there by someone uncaring enough to find a new home for them and instead just letting them fend for themselves. 
 While living at a pond may sound like a dream for these ducks, it will, unfortunately, be the worst and most challenging days of their lives. Not only are there the usual threats, like predators of the forest, but the threats of winter and the cold, harsh temperatures threaten their lives every night. Unlike most wild ducks, they can not fly and find warmer weather someplace else. They have zero shelters from any elements at the moment, as the one tree on their small island has lost all its leaves for the season.  Temperatures are dropping into the teens lately, and I have started finding it hard to sleep at night as I just lay there worried sick about these poor babies.  
 Here is where I could use some help…I and a few others from the community hope to build a quick DIY shelter made from pallets and bales of straw on their island. We have gotten permission from proper authorities to do this; we have the will and perseverance to do this; now, we just need some funding. 
We would need just four pallets, and it’s estimated 13 bales just for the structure to be built. We would need additional straw for roofing and bedding as well. I am highly confident they ( the ten mentioned domestic ducks ) would not only use this shelter but be forever grateful…as would I. 
I am only asking for enough to cover straw bales  (for building and bedding throughout winter, etc.) If there is any extra, it will be used for food and supplies needed to travel to and from the island. 
Thank you to everyone for taking the time to read this. I ask that you consider sharing this, whether that be publicly or with a few close friends who have a soft spot for animals. Truly, anything helps!  I really believe this can save Their lives!

We are a rescue organization that helps the neediest animals in shelters. Our mission statement reflects our belief that all lives should never be forgotten and that all lives matter. We rescue those animals that are continuously overlooked by others and those that need medical help. We love the animals in our care and have been blessed with wonderful volunteers, adopters and supporters.
Little Ruby was pregnant at the shelter and her three babies, Mona, Lisa and Leonardo were born in a wonderful foster home.  Foster Mom Chris gave them all the best of care, and when they were old enough, they came to us.
Ruby went to her forever home quickly and her son Leonardo soon afterward.  Mona and Lisa were still with us, waiting for their forever home, when they were struck with parvo.  Parvo is a killer of puppies; it is deadly and hits with a vicious blow.  Our girls have been in the hospital since 10/26 on intravenous fluids and meds, and receiving constant loving care from the dedicated staff at Nassau Suffolk Animal Hospital. Lisa was seriously ill, could hardly hold her head up and had bloody diarrhea and vomiting.  Mona was in bad shape too, but a bit better than Lisa.
It has been a nightmare to all of us hoping and praying they would be able to be saved, that their little bodies were strong enough to fight off this vicious killer.  Tonight we got word that they started to eat!!  Holding down some food is a tremendous sign of improvement, and we are thrilled.  Their prognosis is better now and we are so relieved.
Our babies have a long road ahead, but it looks like they are progressing in the right direction.  We will do whatever it takes to continue their road to recovery so they may, like their brother Leonardo and Mom Ruby, find a wonderful forever family and enjoy many happy years with them.
Their bills are in the area of $8,000, and any help you can give would be greatly appreciated.  In order to meet our fundraising goal, it will truly take a village.   Any amount you can contribute will make a difference.  Together we can ensure these puppies regain their health and find their loving forever home.
Sincerely,
The Forgotten Friends Family

We are blessed to be alive to share our story. We, Precious McNeil and Marco Allen, are the parents of five young, spirited children: Kaliyah (11), Chloe (7), Grace (5), Demarco (2) and Demar (8 months). Precious works as a 911 dispatch operator and Marco is employed at the local Lowe's store. Together, we have coached soccer, T-ball and other youth sports teams with Parks and Recreation for more than five years. We are a close-knit family that enjoys being part of and contributing to our small, rural community.
This time last week, our thoughts centered on determining the best neighborhood trick-or-treat routes for our children and their cousins. Two days ago, that all changed. Around 2:30 in the morning, our home was consumed by a house fire. Thankfully, our oldest daughter, Kaliyah, awakened in the middle of the night to use the bathroom. When she opened her eyes, she realized something was very wrong: our home was engulfed in thick smoke. Fortunately, a recent fire drill at her school prepared our daughter to act quickly and wisely.
Kaliyah covered her nose and mouth with a bandana, crawled to her mother's bed, screamed her name and shook her to wake her up. Together, they made their way into the living room to locate the other sleeping children amidst the smoke. Remembering where they were earlier in the evening, Kaliyah felt around for Demarco and Grace and carried them out of the house to safety. Precious, Marco and their youngest child followed. Shortly after, when Precious asked about Chloe, without hesitation, Kaliyah ran back into the house to save her sister.
We're stunned and emotional. No words can fully express how thankful we are for Kaliyah's bravery. Her courage and selflessness saved not 1, not 2, not 3, not 4, not 5, not 6, but 7 lives. She is our forever hero. The fire destroyed most of our material possessions, and now our young family is forced to start over, from identifying a new home to ensuring our children have their daily needs met. We welcome any level of support as we work to get back on our feet. From the bottom of our grateful hearts, we thank you for reading our story and helping us to celebrate Kaliyah.

Hi, we're Roxanne & Josh, two devastated cat parents whose hearts have been yo-yo'd over the past few weeks trying to determine what's wrong with our precious little wood ear mushroom, Maitake (Mai).
Our home was blessed on 2/27/21 with the arrival of sweet Mai from our local Humane Animal Rescue in the North Side of Pittsburgh. She means everything to us and her sister mushy, Kikurage.
A few months ago she was diagnosed with gingivitis which we began to treat at home. Realizing that wasn't working, we scheduled an appointment to have her reassessed, at which time she was diagnosed with stomatitis, a gum disease.
Over the next ten days we painstakingly gave her antibiotics. During that time, she declined dramatically and we took her to PVSEC in Pittsburgh. After four days, she's been effectively diagnosed with Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP). This is typically only diagnosed after ruling everything else out, there's no firm test for it. It's generally been thought to be incurable but there's a non-FDA approved drug that could save her life. It's our last resort.
At this time, we're not asking for help with her FIP treatment but for everything that's come before. Admitting a pet to an ER is very expensive and we've already committed to $10,000. First, a $5K Care Credit loan which we were fortunately approved for right away, and an additional $5K that we've charged to our credit cards.
If you've ever met this sweet angel, you'd know that she is the cat everyone hopes to have. When we first admitted her to the ER, they couldn't hear her heartbeat because she was purring so loudly. We just can't let her go and are asking for help to hold onto her as long as we can so we can still afford her FIP medication and continued treatment at the ER vet.
Any help that you can give would be immensely appreciated, we just want our baby home and healthy. Attached is a copy of our latest financial update for reference, feel free to reach out to us with any questions you may have. And please check out FIP Warriors on Facebook and familiarize yourself with the disease. They're seriously doing great work.

We are Friends of Romania (FoR), a U.S. 501(c)(3) Public Charity that seeks to strengthen the two-way alliance between the United States and Romania in the domain of education, culture, diplomacy and shared values. Connecting Jewish Americans of Romanian and Eastern European descent to their roots also figures high on our agenda.
Russia has waged war on Ukraine, forcing millions to find refuge, and we NEED all the help we can get and give. A dramatic situation happened to the orphaned Jewish refugees from Odessa. Please take a moment to read the below, and kindly help us in achieving our goal of alleviating the cold winter months for the orphaned Jewish refugees in Romania and helping them have a meaningful Hanukkah:
In 1993, Tikva first opened its doors in Odesa, Ukraine, with a broad humanitarian mission and an emphasis on reviving a community in this former communist region. Through these efforts, they discovered the plight of local Jewish children suffering homelessness, abuse, neglect or living in bleak and destitute State orphanage environments.
Following their harrowing escape from Odesa, they are now trying their best to maintain their humanitarian mission in Romania, a foreign environment and highly challenging operating conditions. Tikva has, in essence, taken an entire community of almost 1,000 Jewish children from Ukraine and transplanted them (after the first two horrifying weeks of the war) to Romania. Their main objective has been keeping the community together as a family. The hope is that in the absence of their physical community and facilities, they can at least replicate that feeling of home as much as possible while maintaining the psychological cohesiveness and comfort that unity provides. FoR is passionate about providing all the help we can for the Tikva orphanage to survive and thrive in Romania.

Dr. Kevin Pineda, DO, 29 passed away on November 9, 2022.
This fundraiser is to help honor Kevin and create a tribute/memorial to his contributions to the Rutgers PM&R residency program, and all remaining funds will go towards covering the family's funeral expenses.
Kevin was a beloved resident of the Class of '23's Rutger's New Jersey Medical School and Kessler Rehabilitation Residency Program. He provided his patients with the highest quality of care. He always took the time to ensure patients' needs were thoroughly addressed and repeatedly demonstrated sincere compassion and commitment.
In addition to being a great clinician, Kevin was dedicated to his fellow residents and trainees. He took immense pride in sharing his love and knowledge of Osteopathic Medicine and areas of special interest, including musculoskeletal ultrasound, lifestyle medicine, and amputee rehabilitation. He was a devoted teacher to his colleagues, staff and especially medical students. He had an infectious enthusiasm for enjoying many of life’s simple pleasures… food, friends, exercise, and fun. Dr. Pineda was always advocating for changes and improvements. He was engaged in the Medical School representing house staff in Rutgers' Committee of Interns and Residents Union (CIR), and he was well known for his commitment to keeping people safe during the Covid-19 pandemic that culminated in a book chapter of COVID-19 by Cases: A Pandemic Review.
Kevin also touched many lives prior to residency including during his intern year at Morristown Medical Center, his leadership with the Student Osteopathic Medical Association while at TouroCOM – Middletown, and through his various online and in person endeavors. We will remember him the most for his tremendous capacity to give to others and for his unique, heart-warming laugh.

Connie Hauer has been an employee of J&E Companies for the past 10 years and is one of the most dedicated people to her job as Office Manager. She has excelled in her daily duties and does not miss work unless absolutely necessary; until recently. Connie is a single mother who has her daughter and 2 grandchildren living with her whom she helps take care of along with their many pets or “babies” as she calls them. Connie worked hard and was able to purchase her single-family home a number of years ago and it is her pride and joy, after her family. She calls it her castle. As anyone of us who are fortunate enough to own a home, we all know how important it is; but for Connie it is almost twice as important due to how much time she spends at home with her health issues.
Last Wednesday evening Connie requested to leave work a couple hours early to bring her daughter to an appointment. Connie, her daughter and grandchildren were gone for 2 hours and upon their return, she found her castle to be on fire with dense smoke overtaking the home which prevented them from entering. Connie called the fire department and waited to find out the fate of her home and her fur babies that were still trapped inside.
Sadly, due to this fire, she has lost everything, including her 2 dogs and 3 cats that were inside. The home can be replaced but as any pet owner knows, her pets cannot and will forever leave a hole in her heart. A friend has stepped up and taken them in and was able to enter the home after the inspector left to retrieve her babies and give them a proper burial.
As any responsible home owner, Connie does have good insurance but it will not cover all that is needed to rebuild her life. House payments will not stop, not to mention any other financial and emotional hardships she will deal with over the next 6 months that she will be displaced from her home. We are reaching out to ask for any sort of help that can be given to help alleviate some of this burden Connie will be taking on and make things even a little easier for her on her difficult journey ahead.

This is my dog Cocoa Bean. She is a type 1 diabetic who recently went into diabetic shock & has been struggling with diabetic ketoacidosis and pancreatitis. She had become insulin resistant to the type of insulin we were giving her and I did not know, so basically it was like she wasn’t getting her medicine for well over a month. A diabetic, especially a type one, not getting insulin resulted in her becoming extremely sick and developing ketones and pancreatitis. On the night before Halloween, she was rushed to the animal hospital where she spent four days consistently in the hospital undergoing multiple surgeries, treatments, and medicines to get her to a safe point of continuing care at home. After 4 days of continuous hospital care we managed to get her ketones down from moderate to small even though her sugar is still uncontrolled, and she was still labeled an uncontrolled diabetic. They let her come home, and now it requires a lot of care, attention, medicine, and treatments to continue monitoring her glucose levels, getting her to controlled levels again, and giving her the type of insulin she now needs. Every two weeks I have to replace a sensor on her back which alerts me if her levels go to alarming amounts, to prevent anything like this from happening again in the future. Unfortunately, all of these things that she needs to help her, including the literal insulin she needs every single day to keep her alive, costs extreme amounts of money, especially without pet insurance. She’s more than just a dog, she’s family and my best friends and I promised her I would try my best & do anything I need to do to get her better. I’m already well over $10,000 in bills from being in the hospital for four continuous days, so I can’t stop now. Anything donated would be incredibly appreciated in helping me afford her insulin, her sensors, and her pancreatitis treatments. Scar is a beautiful grey boy kitty who was left behind when his owners moved out. Sadly, I found Scar inside a trash can looking for food. (I think he had climbed in it.) 
I fed him salmon, which he devoted in 2 seconds. 
He was skinny, barely walking, and looked really ill. So I decided to try to save him and hoped I could find him a good home.
I have two cats already, but I could make room for a third.
I made a game plan: take him to the vet and get his shots up to date, test him for FeLV and FIV, and get him neutered.
The FIV Diagnosis
What I didn't plan for was the FIV diagnosis.
FIV is like HIV but for cats and is passed through deep bites. Unfortunately, Scar was an inside/outside cat, and this is what exposed him to FIV.
At first, the vet said he had a fever but it could have been due to the stress of living on the streets. Then the diagnosis came in and she told me my options which included euthanasia.
Euthanasia is not an option UNLESS he is so ill that he is suffering. Scar, for now, is not that ill, and the antibiotics should work fine for him.
I am now desperate and determined to find Scar a home where he will be an inside-only cat. And until I do, keep him alive and, of course, safely separated from my other two cats.
I can still care for him, but I only have a small space to keep him in, which isn't great for cats--but it is safe for him.
I've already spent around $500 on Scar and have had a few generous donations to help with that.
The vet bill was $225-ish, which included his vaccinations, deworming medicine, an antibiotic for an infection, and the tests for FeLV and FIV.
The rest was spent on supplies like a fluffy grey blanket, and Tiki cat foot because this cat deserves some really nice food that he loves.

Daniel Lang and his fiancé, Ian McELyea, were victims of an apartment fire on Saturday, October 29, 2022. Here is their story:
“On Saturday night/Sunday morning, we went to a Halloween party with some friends and stayed out later than usual or otherwise, we would have been in bed asleep. At 1:21 am, we were dancing at the party, and our downstairs neighbors called us and said, “Hurry home!!” I could hear the emergency sirens in the background. We rushed home as quickly as possible. We were forced to park two blocks away because there were dozens of emergency vehicles. We ran to our home as dozens of people came out of their homes to watch our home burn down… Dozens of firefighters were there. Firefighters took pickaxes to the walls; they cut a hole in the roof to let out the smoke. They smashed all the windows and hosed the place down from the ceiling. They had first to cut off the electricity and gas. We sat in the driveway and cried as they brought dead body after body out. We lost two cats, a snake, a salamander, and ten lizards. By God’s Grace: Sabrina rose from the ashes, and one lizard was spared. Sabrina spent two days in the hospital and is stable and with us. The lizard appears to be stable. All personal belongings are destroyed. The fire marshal investigator determined the source of the fire was an electrical failure in a jerryrigged 220 space heater outlet that our landlord knew was faulty. This 220 overloaded a failing breaker. All light bulbs exploded, and all outlets caught fire and melted. The fire damage follows the electrical lines. The landlord did not provide us with smoke detectors and did not address the electrical issues he knew about. We are alive today because our friend invited us to a Halloween party.”
Please consider helping Daniel and Ian to cover medical expenses for their animals as well as to help re-establish their home and belongings.

Violeta B. Firmalino passed away on Saturday, October 8, 2022 at age 64 in Long Beach, CA surrounded by family. 
Violeta was born on May 22, 1958 in San Gregorio, Laguna, Philippines — the 7th of 8 children to Anselmo and Teodorica Belen. 
She attended local De Mesa Elementary School prior to moving to Manila where she enrolled at University of the East for high school. She then attended University of Perpetual Help for college before immigrating to the United States in 1979 to join her mother and siblings.  
Once in the US, Violeta attended Long Beach City College where she completed programs for nursing assistant and medical secretary. She did not stop there; she continued to enroll in leisure classes such as in the culinary arts throughout the years. 
Violeta married Manuel Firmalino in 1987 settling in in Long Beach, CA where she later gave birth to their only son, John Emmanuel Belen Firmalino.
Violeta worked for Long Beach Memorial/Miller’s Children and Women’s as a Patient Care Assistant for nearly 25 years. She served tens of thousands of new borns and their parents until her retirement in 2015.
In her retirement, Violeta continued to enjoy her usual pastimes; gardening, cooking, reading about current events, and most of all, spending time with her family. Violeta was also an active parishioner at St. Barnabas Catholic Church where she was a member of the Handmaids of the Lord group and the Filipino-American Association. She attended mass weekly as well as different days throughout the week in adoration of the Blessed Sacrament. 
Her impact everyone she met was nothing short of positive. Violeta loved meeting new people and getting to know them upon their first introduction. She will forever be missed by family, friends and everyone she has met throughout her life.

The sliders had blown out, so they walked into a mess of sea mud and belongings, many not even their own. The realization began to set in: the house wasn't in the hurricane- the hurricane was in the house.
The only choice was and still is to focus on the small moments- step by step, they configure what has happened and what needs to. Every day has been spent dragging out the contents of what once made their house a home.
With a total loss incurred, I ask for your support for Julie. Many friends have asked what they can do to help. It's a question Julie hasn't been able to answer. From socks to a new living space, any amount you can share will allow her to begin to rebuild.
Thank you from the bottom of the sea to the top of the winds.

We are humbly asking for any assistance in putting to rest this beautiful soul who touched so many.. My brother, along with Jen's sister and mother are facing some extremely hard times both emotionally and financially. Anything helps.

My name is Angela Tyler and I'm raising money to give my daughter's cat, Finley, a second blood transfusion in an attempt to save his life.
Finley was gifted to my daughter on her birthday after her dad suddenly passed away in 2020. The new addition to our family was a source of laughter and playfulness in some of the hardest months of our lives, isolating after such a loss. To say Finley is special to us is an understatement. 
Last week I realized that Finley wasn't acting like himself and wasn't eating, drinking, or moving around much. At one point he lost control of his bladder and seemed to go into shock. I rushed him to the Animal Hospital where we discovered he was anemic. He underwent a blood transfusion and came home the following day. His first checkup looked okay, not great, but the second checkup his numbers had dropped. Yesterday he stopped eating and drinking.
Today I've called our vet and the Animal Hospital. They said sometimes when an animal goes anemic they need multiple transfusions and their only suggested course of action is another blood transfusion. They estimated another $1.5k - $2k on top of the $2.2k I'd spent the first time.
I've exhausted my financial resources and decided to make a last-ditch effort on social media. To my surprise there's so much interest, I decided to make this GoFundMe instead of relying on CashApp so it's easier for everyone to see the progress and make the donation.
If I'm not able to raise enough or if we still lose him, the funds will be applied to the medical bills from his first transfusion and/or used to memorialize him somehow for my daughter.
If you're just able to share, that still means the world to us.
Thank you so much for your help & support.

Help defend the First Amendment and Freedom of the Press! The Erie Reader, Erie's only independent, locally-owned alternative newspaper, and its contributing editor, Jim Wertz, were sued for defamation by PA State Senator Dan Laughlin, who filed a multi-million dollar lawsuit against the Reader and Wertz. The lawsuit alleges that Wertz defamed Laughlin in an opinion piece outlining actions connected to attempts to overturn the results of the 2020 Election and the events of January 6. This lawsuit is an attempt to silence the media from publishing critical political commentary and analysis.
"The First Amendment and the Pennsylvania Constitution provide robust protection for individuals and entities to gather, report, publish, and comment on accurate information that is a matter of public concern or significance," wrote Paula Knudsen Burke, a lawyer for the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press in a July 25 response to Congressman Mike Kelly, who first threatened litigation over the opinion piece. "The Op-Ed falls squarely within the scope of those important constitutional protections."
The Erie Reader and Jim Wertz have retained the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and attorneys from Saul Ewing Arnstein & Lehr in Pittsburgh, PA, to defend them from Senator Laughlin's suit. While some of the attorney's fees have been graciously provided pro-bono, additional fees will be sizable and unavoidable.
Help these independent journalists maintain their voice in their community by contributing to the Erie Reader Legal Defense Fund. The First Amendment and the future of journalism may depend on it.

Hi, my name is Jason. My Family and I recently had a house fire on 10/11/2022 around 12:30 a.m. We are currently in a hotel, but everyone is safe and not harmed.
Late at night on Monday, October 10th, I was streaming some on twitch. The rest of my family was asleep. I started to smell something burning and thought it was cold outside, so it’s typical to smell things like this in my neighborhood as the neighbors use a fireplace. Still, I said to the twitch chat I smelled something burning, and even though I think it’s the neighbor's fireplace, it’s always better to be safe than sorry, so I’ll brb going to check around the house.
I walked around the house for about 30 seconds investigating and thought I better wake up my family members so they could check around since it did seem like the smell was coming from inside the house. Upon us walking into our living room, I flicked on the light, and we saw the room had a fair bit of smoke filling it up, but we couldn’t tell from where.
The smell was getting stronger by this time too. I proceeded to check more of the house. As I turned on the kitchen light, I noticed the smoke was really thick in the kitchen, and I instantly started to look over towards the stove, oven, coffee pot etc., just assuming that would be a likely place to have smoke emitting,
As I got closer to those appliances, I was not seeing anything, but then I looked to the left at the basement door, and it looked like a full-blown factory smoke stack with a thick dark rolling cloud of smoke just blasting out from it. This all was happening within seconds, and I instantly spoke out loud OH GOD, THE HOUSE IS ON FIRE HELP US as I turned around going to my room, yelling down the hallway the house is on fire call 911, we gotta get out,
As all of this was happening, I had already been having problems breathing coming from the kitchen with all of that smoke. As I went down my hallway to open the door to my room which was closed, I was surprised and frightened to see my room filling with a crazy amount of thick dark smoke. My tv was flickering, and the ceiling was black. Small little holes in my walls from nails, thumb tacks etc., had smoke just spewing out, sort of like a tea kettle that is boiling. My room looked like it was being cooked and about to burst into flames at any moment.
A thought crossed my head for seconds. “What do I do? What do I grab? I’m about to lose everything I own” panicking and being overwhelmed, unable to breathe. I quickly decided none of this stuff matters. Everyone needs to get out now. This is life and death.
I quickly grabbed my phone, two shirts and a pair of shorts that was sitting on my bed, sticking them over my face hoping to breathe better as I gasped for breath stumbling around in shock, saying out loud again, “Oh God, Please help us” I stumbled out of my room and yelled down the hallway again GET OUT NOW THE HOUSE IS LOST. By this time, I was so disoriented and oxygen-deprived that I fell over as I left my room, trying to escape the house. I felt so lightheaded that I was close to passing out, needing to get fresh air. I dropped my phone and tripped over a box, and fell about three times trying to get up and crawl to the front door just 15 feet away. I managed to get up, leaving my phone in the middle of the floor.
I was finally out of the house and able to breathe. One of my family members started calling 911. As I came down the steps of my porch and tried to collect myself and my breath, I heard my other family member calling from the living room, so I quickly marched right back into the house, which was completely pitch black and filled with smoke at this point, you couldn’t see anything. It was absolutely terrifying. We were both falling down low, and I felt their arm which I grabbed probably way too hard. I had them, they were okay, but we needed to get out.
I still couldn’t fully breathe. I quickly walked out and yelled to the rest of my family for help. So they put the phone down and ran into the house. I heard the 911 operator on the phone, so I grabbed it and started to speak with them, giving the home address, telling them I could see my remaining family members coming out of the house etc.
Seeing everyone out of the house and safe was such a relief. Even though my house was on fire and we were about to lose everything we owned, I didn’t care. All that mattered was seeing everyone outside safe, walking around, and no one was harmed or burned etc. everyone seemed to be breathing okay, and the fire department was on the way. I stood there thanking god for helping us all escape unharmed. My family means everything to me, and losing one of them would have never left me the same.
We stood around collecting ourselves, and the firefighters arrived within about 10 minutes. If I had to guess, I’m really not sure how long it was, but they got there pretty quickly. They dispatched three trucks full of firefighters from three different stations, and there were probably about 25 to 30 firefighters. They quickly got dressed in their suits, got their hoses, and started to work on putting out the fire which was blazing in the basement.
While they were fighting it, there was a person speaking with us about things we needed to do, asking questions about the home, insurance, hotel, food etc. the firefighters had to bust out all of our basement windows and remove the security bars from them as well they busted out a window upstairs and had large fans positioned around pulling out smoke. They cut the power to the house, as well the water too. I think it took them about 30 minutes to put the fire out fully, spraying water around in the basement.
After about 2 hours, they told us the house could not be lived in any longer. It was not safe. They said they think the fire started around the washer and dryer 220-watt electrical outlet, which is directly under my room. My room has a few holes burned through the floor that is large, you can look up and see my bed through them, my tv stand fell in a hole and was turned over, and another large hole had a bunch of various cables for my pc, xbox etc. hanging through it.
They let us go into the house to get some personal belongings out and things that thieves might target etc., but they told us not to enter my room as the floor can’t be trusted. The house has extensive fire damage in the basement. A lot of the flooring will need to be replaced, the electrical and plumbing will all need to be replaced, and there is major smoke damage throughout the entire house. They informed us all our food would need to be thrown away, medicine, canned goods, etc., anything plastic. It’s wild. They even said sealed canned goods and 2 liters of soda, medicine containers and whatnot. All of that stuff gets penetrated by the smoke and is unsafe. We had so much food that was being tossed, and it was a shame.
The inspector looked at the home and said he has been doing this for 25 years and doesn’t understand how the fire stopped where it did and why the entire house didn’t go up. We think God stopped it where he wanted it to stop. It’s a miracle looking at the aftermath. The fire was hot enough to melt the metal shelving we had on the inner wall, but yet didn’t consume the entire wall or spread to boxes and other things easily flammable right next to it, which it should have and spread to the rest of the house. You can see in the picture where the fire stopped and didn’t spread any further. It’s wild to me you can see our basement walls and ceiling burnt and fell, the air ducts burnt, in the room to the right, the massive PVC pipe plumbing is drooped down melted, electrical wiring etc., but to the left, the boxes and other stuff never caught. It’s a good thing, too, because further in that room, we had some high-power rifle ammunition from a gun collection that could have gone off like a bomb sending out shrapnel.
The room to the right is where they think it started, and it goes far back. There were clothes hanging in there. And some were brand new. Some were old. There were Jackets, suits, all sorts of things, just all destroyed.
Thankfully everyone got out of the house safe, and no one was harmed. Everything else is replaceable. We are fortunate to have insurance which should really help us recover our home in time. We are going on over two weeks living in a hotel at the moment, things are awkward, but we are doing great, all things considered. Insurance expects us not to be in our home for 6 to 8 months. Currently, they are trying to look for a rental home for us to live in temporarily. 
Thanks to my streaming, I can rewatch the VOD and see the time stamp of when I mentioned I smelled something burning til my stream ended, which was on its own via my electrical wires melting. It was just 4 minutes. Just that quickly, everything happened. I’ve always thought to myself in my head, if there were a fire, I would do this, or I would do that, I would be fine. Well, let me tell you, the movies don’t do the real thing justice. We were overwhelmed in such a short amount of time. I Thank God for helping us get out, and I am so happy I was awake that night because had I been asleep, everyone likely would have died. You never know when a day might be your last. Be sure to stay on good terms with the people you care about. Let them know you love them.

Hello, my name is Conor, and recently my best friend and family member Clementine, who is only 5 years old, has been diagnosed with a terminal illness called chronic kidney disease. The search for answers and diagnosis has broken my heart and my bank account. Please read.
The Timeline:
Feb 18th Regular Vet - $316.43: Clementine is seen by her regular vet because she's been vomiting frequently for a couple of weeks, not just regular hairballs or scarf and barfs, but liquid. An examination and blood work is done. She is prescribed a short-term antiemetic+antibiotic. The vet emails me about the blood work and says:
"Normal blood cell counts, blood chemistry panel and urinalysis. No signs of metabolic or systemic disease."*
This turns out to be untrue, which was explained to me by the Doctor I see on 10/20 (8 months later!!!)*. However, she recovers well with the antiemetic, and the excess vomiting ceases. So at this point, I still suspect nothing serious.
(*Side note, I want to make it clear, I'm not accusing any veterinarians of malicious intent or wilful misconduct, the problem is within the system of categories, conduct and protocols on the subject of kidney disease. The current protocols has put veterinarians just doing their job and following guidelines in the unfortunate position of ignoring blatant kidney disease (extremely common killer of cats!) and sending patients on an expensive wild goose chase that can make things worse.)
Fast forward to June, I started noticing Clementine being very picky with her food, refusing to eat it all or refusing certain types outright. For her 5 years with me, she's been pretty exclusively a wet-food cat, I thought maybe she was just getting tired of eating the same old stuff, so I tried some dry food (which she's almost never been given), and she ate it up. I figure it's just a phase, and keep trying new foods, with the dry food as a backup.
By 7/2 this had escalated to outright refusal of all food and water. After a full 24 hours of not eating or urinating and a night's rest with no change - I rushed her to Urgent care.
7/3: Urgent Care Animal Hospital - $681 - Diagnosed with some inflammation in the bladder, possible mild struvite crystals, given pain medication and mirtazapine. Told to keep her medicated so she'll eat only wet food and drink water to normalize her. Veterinarians suggest she might be peeing elsewhere or getting food elsewhere that I'm not aware of; I adamantly refuse the possibility of this but got the impression they thought they knew better. Reacts well to medicine but returns to refusing food after five days or so of being off. It should be noted that blood work was done yet again here, and in combination with her symptoms, pointed to kidney disease, and yet again, an entirely different set of veterinarians made no suggestion of kidney disease to me. At this point, I don't even have "kidney disease" on my radar. I'm trusting the vets, I'm not a doctor.
7/13: Regular Vet Followup- Xrays are done - $375: Finds nothing wrong. About Sebastian Mejia ヽ༼ຈل͜ຈ༽ノ
Sebastian Mejía, 24, of Miami, Florida, passed away unexpectedly on October 6th, 2022, while completing his Fulbright Research Program in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
Sebastian was born on May 9th, 1998, in Miami, Florida, to Colombian immigrants Rosa Elena Martínez Bethés and Jaime Mejía Londoño. He grew up in Miramar, Florida, and attended Pembroke Pines Charter Elementary School. He enjoyed playing video games like Pokémon and Super Smash Bros., and he was a soccer goalie as a kid. In 2008, His family moved to Naples, Florida, where he lived in the Golden Gate Estates and attended Corkscrew Elementary School and Corkscrew Middle School. In 2016 he graduated Summa Cum Laude from Palmetto Ridge High School, where he worked as a cafeteria worker and participated in the swim, band, and childcare programs.
Out of his own volition, Sebastian conducted genealogical research to learn more about the Muisca and Panche people, from whom he is a descendant. Interested in reconnecting with his ancestors' community, language, and culture, he began to research the Muisca’s history and their struggle for recognition as an Indigenous community in Colombia. While doing this personal research, he came across similar movements in Brazil and immediately developed an interest in the plurality of the movements and the similarities between the two countries. Alongside his friends, he organized a grassroots and community-based organization, 718 Coalition, committed to community empowerment, education, abolition, and liberation from all forms of violence for marginalized people.
He received Florida’s Academic Scholars Award to attend Florida State University, graduating Summa Cum Laude in May 2020 with a dual bachelor’s degree in Latin American and Caribbean Studies and International Affairs with a minor in Portuguese. During his undergraduate studies, he worked as an English instructor and childcare provider in Managua, Nicaragua, as a teacher and tutor in Tallahassee and Naples, volunteered with the Tallahassee Bail Fund and the Frenchtown Urban Farm, served as the public relations chair for the Hispanic/Latinx Student Union, was the membership chair and secretary for Leaders Empowering Others in Needs of Education and Service, and was the co-founder, Director, and Event Coordinator for the Coalition for Latinx Studies at FSU.
For his strong academic track record, he was awarded a myriad of grants and fellowships, including the Foreign Language & Area Studies Fellowship and Service Scholars Award, and participated in nationally competitive academic programs such as the Moore Undergraduate Research Apprentice Program, the University of Florida’s Language and Culture Program in Rio, and Middlebury’s Portuguese Language Program. Sebastian collaborated with communities as he undertook archival and ethnographic fieldwork in Brazil and in his Abuelita’s hometown of Albán, Cundinamarca, Colombia. He completed his undergraduate senior thesis entitled “Decolonizing Land & Re-indigenizing Body: The Recuperation of Indigenous Identity in Brazil,” which analyzes how communities who have been socially and politically “whitened” affirm their Indigenous identities and rights to ancestral lands while redefining the parameters of indigeneity in conflict with the Brazilian state. He situated this conflict within neoliberal multiculturalism and historicized the tensions between the Brazilian state and resistant communities.
In the spring of 2021, Sebastian was awarded a Departmental Fellowship at New York University and began his graduate studies at the Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies at NYU that fall. Throughout his graduate studies, he was interested in and engaged in work related to indigeneity, ethnic and land recognition, social movements, multiculturalism, and the ways that processes of capitalism impact Indigenous communities in Brazil and Colombia. In 2022, Sebastian was in the process of finishing up his master’s degree in Latin American and Caribbean Studies while also completing his Fulbright Research Program under the mentorship of faculty from the Institute of History at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro. He began taking orfebrería classes and enjoyed creating jewelry. He was awarded a Tinker Foundation Field Research Grant to further his interdisciplinary research, traveling to archival sites in São Paulo and Brasília, and was accepted to PhD preview programs at Brown, Princeton, and Yale. Through a social history lens, he tackled questions that grounded his analysis in the narratives of those affected. Sebastian was in the process of completing his master's thesis, “Indigeneity, Land, & Concessions: A Transnational Comparative History of Indigenous Identity, (De)colonization, and Neoliberal Multiculturalism in Brazil and Colombia,” and his research project for his Fulbright program tentatively titled, “Land & Indigeneity: The Dissolution of Indigenous Lands and the Struggle for Ethnic Recognition and Territorial Demarcation.”
Before his untimely passing, Sebastian was in the process of applying to PhD programs where he would obtain his doctorate in History, preferably at the University of Texas at Austin. Through his work, he hoped to continue to push fields that engaged with Indigenous communities to be connected to the critical struggle of decolonization. He wanted to become a professor to carry on the kind of transformative teaching he had already engendered with his loved ones.
Sebastian is deeply loved by many. He cherished his family and friends like no one else and expressed his love in his own unique way. His humor and wit were and still are unmatched, and he would constantly make his friends and family, and himself, laugh without trying. From a young age, Sebastian was always making friends; so much so that there were friends of his who never met and, in the same vein, friends of his who only met because of him. He valued community tremendously and was constantly cultivating it wherever he was. He generously shared everything he learned with his family and friends; he taught his little sister how to swim, he taught his brothers about teamwork, and he taught his parents that they are deserving of peace. He wanted nothing more than to make sure his family and friends were okay. He wanted them to succeed and find purpose. He offered guidance wherever he could and asked for help in areas he struggled. He cared for everyone and did everything he could to make sure his parents, especially, would be taken care of. Sebastian really just wanted to be happy and make sure his loved ones were happy. No amount of words will ever encompass how layered and interesting and worthy of a person Sebastian was.
Sebastian’s spirit will forever live on through his parents Rosa and Jaime, his older brother Camilo, his younger brothers Alejandro and Daniel, and his younger sister Catalina. They love him so much.

Emerald Monbulk wildlife Shelter
Emerald Monbulk Wildlife shelter in the Dandenong Ranges is run by the incredibly dedicated Carol Seeger.
Carol has been caring for injured and orphaned wildlife for over 30 years. On any given day, it’s not unusual to have several hundreds of animals on the property (aka mouths to feed and care for).
Sadly, there is very little support in running a wildlife shelter. Carol takes in orphaned, displaced and injured native animals daily and gets no funding. Everything is paid for out of her (and her long-suffering husband Mark’s) pocket. Our volunteers assist with bringing in supplies; however the costs associated with running a shelter at this scale are incredibly substantial. Carol being the generous person she is, rarely asks for help.
What costs are associated with running the Shelter?
Formula for our young macropods and marsupials is vital to their well-being and development - a 20kg bag costs over $500. We make up multiple litres of formula daily and go through these bags every few weeks. On top of this we need a constant supply (many kgs) of fruit and vegetables for our birds and possums, meat and insects for our omnivorous and carnivorous birds, and general staples such as seed and pellets. In addition to this, we have the behind-the-scenes costs of running such a set-up - including; water and electricity bills, medications and vet expenses, infrastructure and building materials for adequate housing/enclosures, as well as travel and petrol costs associated with rescues and wildlife transport.
What kind of animals does the shelter care for?
We care for everything from Eastern grey kangaroos, swamp wallabies and bare-nosed wombats to blue tongue lizards, parrots and even the occasional sugar glider and echidna.
A shelter success story..
In early July 2022 one of our rescuers was called out to an adult brushtail possum who had been hit by a car and left on the road. After being assessed by a vet, she came to us with soft tissue swelling around her spine, a pelvic fracture and a concussion. Her prognosis was not great. We moved her into a comfortable aviary and administered pain relief and fluids. She instantly became a favourite amongst volunteers for her sweet personality and love of kale (and mealworms). Often possums get a bad rap due to their displacement in urban environments - they seek shelter in roofs and gardens as much of their natural habitat has been disturbed. You will find though, that possums are full of charm, personality and cheekiness.
In late July, our beautiful brushtail was picking up. She was much brighter and gained her balance and movement back. We also noticed that she had gained quite a bit of weight! Just as we were contemplating putting her on Jenny Craig, we noticed our lovely lady actually had a newborn joey in her pouch. The excitement of watching such an incredible recovery, as well as now seeing a healthy baby, was such a miracle. The great news didn’t stop there, however - a few weeks later, we discovered that our miracle baby was in fact, twins! The occurrence of twins in brushtail possums is incredibly rare - so the fact that our, now affectionately named ‘Mama Poss’ survived being hit by a car and carried on two have two bubs is truly incredible. Being in care has allowed her the safety and substantial nutrients needed to care for two young. A task that would be incredibly difficult for her in the wild where food is often scarce. Part of our improved infrastructure and care plan for Mama Poss has included the build of a large soft-release aviary where she can continue to raise her babies until they are old enough to care for themselves. As possums occupy territories, this set-up was done at a release site nearby. This requires considerable planning and logistics both from the build perspective and in terms of care and food supply.
What does a day look like at the Shelter?
Our morning crew of volunteers arrive around 8:30am. They will start by prepping formula and making up bottles for the orphaned joeys in care. On any given day, there could be 20-30+ joeys (kangaroos, wombats and possums) and a further 10-15+ adolescents, all requiring multiple milk feeds. These numbers spike during spring when young are born and tragically separated from their mums (either through road accidents, cat and dog attacks or natural disasters).
Once the morning feeds are complete, healthy babies are taken outside to stretch their legs, enjoy some sun and learn that the outside world isn't so scary.
Meanwhile, our volunteers start cleaning out and disinfecting all of the baby enclosures as well as washing and drying the many pouches we go through daily. Our washing machine runs approximately 10 hours out of the day with the hundreds of towels, pouches, blankets and beds that we wash per week).
We prep fruit and vegetables for our adult animals awaiting release and our resident birds. We go through kilos of fresh produce each shift.
Meat meals are made up for our meat eating birds. This includes kookaburras, magpies, tawny frogmouths, butcher birds and the occasional water bird. A large number of these birds come into care after being displaced as young or as adults who have been hit by cars while catching insects at dusk. Sadly, car headlights attract flying insects, creating a dangerous feeding ground for our nocturnal birds.
Once all food is prepped, it is onto cleaning all outside enclosures and flight aviaries. This includes a thorough clean of all floors, feeding and water stations. Aviaries are then re-stocked with fresh foliage, fruits, vegetables and seeds. This ensures enrichment for the birds. Our juvenile kangaroos and wombats also get fed their bottles and supplementary food while they are transitioning to living in the wild.
Ongoing foliage collection is a mammoth task and vital to our animals' health and wellbeing. Our dedicated volunteers collect fresh native foliage and flowers daily to ensure our birds and possums are supplied with as much of their natural diet as possible. We also rely heavily on a few kind neighbours who provide freshly cut grass every few days.
Our morning crew usually finish up around 1pm before our afternoon volunteers arrive. Our afternoon team will commence the second round of feeds in the early afternoon. This often includes another 20-30 bottles. Once all babies are fed, they are brought back inside for the evening, where they are nice and warm. In addition, we often have a number of baby birds that require constant feeding throughout the day - and they definitely let you know! Our afternoon crew also attend to all of our juvenile and adult ringtail and brushtail possums. As per our other enclosures, this includes a thorough clean, fresh foliage, water, fruit and vegetables. We get dozens of calls to take in baby possums as small as 50g who require milk every 3 hours.
The above happens daily - rain, hail or shine. We have a full roster of volunteers who help out 7 days a week as it is a 24/7 job. Carol is always on call - whether it is overnight feeding, pouch checks or rescues, she truly never gets a break. Carol has dedicated her life to helping our incredible native animals and always does so with a smile, incredible warmth, and empathy.
We rely on your generosity to help Carol and her volunteers continue to care for our beautiful wildlife. Every dollar helps us make change in these animals' lives and also allows us to continue to educate the public about how special our Australian wildlife is.
How will your donations be used?
Building new enclosures and aviaries
Maintenance and improving current enclosures for animals
Setting up safe release sites for the animals raised in our care

Precious Paws needs your help!  I know that we have been asking a lot of everyone who sees our posts and go-fund-me items.  We are very grateful and appreciative of everything we have gotten from everyone.  We can’t say thank you loud enough!  
As much as we hate to ask again, we are.
Precious Paws is volunteer based shelter that receives funding from 3 local municipalities when their police departments bring stray, abandoned, sick or injured animals.  The monies we receive per animal is minimal and doesn’t cover the cost of medications, foods, litter or any of the day-to-day things these animals require.  We are glad that these animals are brought to us so we can begin their journeys to getting healthy and get new homes, however the majority of them come in with medical needs.    
This is the second time this year that our shelter volunteers have surprised to literally find kittens stuffed in a box or carrier left outside.  The first time there were 7 kittens left who were about 8 weeks old. 
On Friday of last week, someone dropped a small carrier covered up with a blanket under the mailbox.    It was dropped off between when the morning cleaning volunteers leave around 10:30 and the afternoon volunteers arrive around 1:30.  Video shows that the vehicle had driven in and around the shelter area numerous times waiting for the morning staff to leave.  
As our volunteers opened the small carrier and started taking out the kittens, we were stunned, shocked and sickened.  Stuffed inside this small pen were 8 baby kittens about 5 weeks old.  Each one that we took out was covered in fecal matter, goopy eyes that were almost sealed shut from conjunctivitis and starving for food.   Each kitten immediately was washed down with a damp cloth and their eyes wiped clean so they could open them.  Once cleaned up enough to get a look at them it was clear that these babies would need to be taught how to eat on their own since mama was not with them.  
The gray and white runt of the litter couldn’t eat on it’s own so we immediately took it to the kitchen where we started feeding it with a syringe. Finally with a full tummy, the kitten was resting in a soft bed with the other 7 while we were reaching out to one of our foster families to see if they could take on the smallest one.  Without hesitation, our foster family agreed to take the kitten; so our manager jumped in her car to meet the family halfway to Proctor.  
Throughout the night the kitten seemed to be doing okay, but by 6am it was not wanting to eat much.  An emergency trip to a vet showed that the baby had upper respiratory issues and was given nasal sprays to help keep the passages open.  This visit alone was upwards of $350.  The baby was also given something to help stimulate its appetite.  Back at the foster’s home the kitten wasn’t showing any improvements and it lost it battle to live that evening. 
We still can’t fathom why would anyone take 8 nursing kittens away from their mother and abandon them at a shelter when no one was there.  They could have knocked on the door when volunteers were there instead of leaving them hungry, sick and full of their own stools for another several hours when the afternoon staff arrived.  
As we said, we need your help, in addition to the vet bills for the one we lost, we will need vetting for the conjunctivitis, possible upper respiratory and whatever else the stool samples tell us is wrong with these babies.  We will now be these babies “mama” for at least the next 8 weeks, hoping to find them homes after that time.  The kittens will need to be all vaccinated for rabies and distemper, spay or neutered and microchipped as part PP procedures.  
This year so far, we have spent over $6,400 just in spay and neuter vet costs.  The other vetting costs this year is well over $5000, which includes vaccinations, ear mite and bacterial ear infections medications, flea treatments, broken bones on kittens, upper respiratory infections and other contagious sicknesses that have come in.  Add in the daily expenses of food, litter and cleaning supplies, and you will see that the nominal fees we get from the contracted municipalities doesn’t cover much.
We fundraise, receive donations and give out of our pockets to help these animals find their furever homes.  The adoption fees don’t cover our expenses, so we are reaching out asking for your generous donations.  Please, please, please help us to continue to help the animals that are entrusted to us to save their lives.  We need your help now more than ever.

Dominic Albert Drummond passed away on November 17, 2022, in Sutter Hospital in Sacramento, California with his parents, Teresa Drummond and Al Drummond, by his side.
